title: Nemesis Games
author: James S.A. Corey
review:
This is the best book in the series yet. The tone of this entry is different from previous entries and does a much better job of providing depth to the characters of the Rocinante that we've spent time with but have never really gotten to get to know beyond Holden. The writing style has been refined and really rounded out some of the weaker points of some of the other novels in the series.

Previous entries while entertaining and knowing where the plot should go slightly struggled in the characterization of some of the individuals involved. Hopefully the series keeps up with providing better motivations for its characters, this entry was stellar and really ups the stakes. The biggest con of this entry is the major event that occurs is somewhat hard to believe would happen in a technologically advanced planet, but has eerie parallels to 9/11 that kind of brings up the plausibility in a strange way. The series does have a problem with antagonist motivations, hopefully this is elucidated more as the plot continues.

title: Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking
author: Malcolm Gladwell
review: I listened to this book via the audiobook. I enjoyed the first half of the book and then it does become a little repetitive and easy to zone out listening to. It was enjoyable as a kind of extended podcast, but there aren't many conclusions that fall out from the book that you can really take action on in terms of our unconscious decision making, just more about being aware of your unconscious decision making, which can be unfulfilling. The book is worth listening to, but it can have a bit of filler content.

title: East of Eden
author: John Steinbeck
review:
I originally read this book about 10 years ago when I was starting college and for some reason felt compelled to read again. This is a book that really sticks with you, it is stark reflection of the human condition and the battle we all face between choosing to be good or choosing to be evil. It's one of those books that takes on different meanings in different phases of life, and I feel like I have new things to take away from this book after reading it in this phase of life that I didn't have when I read it 10 years ago.

The only real criticism I have of this book is that I wish it was longer; which is strange to say, since it's not a short book, but you do grow attached to these characters and want to continue to see what happens to them. There's also a few points where characters are at seemingly critical turning points but then meet an early demise, usually due to sickness or accidents. This part does reflect early 20th century life where disease and accidents were a more regular occurrence, but it does make you wonder what could have been. Perhaps this is another lesson to take away from this book as well, where your story can end where you don't expect.

title: Cannery Row
author: John Steinbeck
review:
The slice of life described in Cannery Row is a contrast to the epic East of Eden, but I wanted to read more Steinbeck and explore his poetic descriptions of Monterey. Although Cannery Row doesn't have a conventional plot with a traditional beginning, middle, and end you do get the experience of accompanying several characters that are all fairly down on their luck and struggling to find meaning in life.

There are themes of these characters pining for the fleeting moments in their past where they experienced beauty either in the love of a beautiful woman, a marriage that was brief and tumultuous, or lucrative business deals that turned sour. The Cannery Row district is fairly rough and tumble as described here, but there is an unbridled optimism that shines through in classic Steinbeck fashion in the societal ties that bind this nontraditional community.

There are some real poetic passages in this novel that are quite lovely to experience and in general this book is just a pleasure to read as long as you have the expectation that it's not about the destination but of being a part of this community and peering through the briefly illuminated windows in these characters' lives.

title: Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup

review: I would recommend watching the HBO special over this book if you're interested in the subject matter and want a more concise overview. However, a lot of the details of this book are fascinating and disturbing that were never mentioned in the HBO documentary.

title: Babylon’s Ashes
author: James S.A. Corey
review:
Almost did not finish, the quality of this entry compared to the previous is jarring. Not a ton of interesting events happen compared to Nemesis Games and the personal motivations of the crew of the Rocinante are almost completely discarded aside from Naomi. The number of POV characters in this novel also work against it as we're spending time with characters which are frankly not as interesting or invested in as the core cast and don't have a lasting impact on the outcome.

The ending was also not very surprising and could see it coming from about the book's midpoint with only a couple of minor surprises along the way. Overall, pretty disappointing book compared to the quality of Nemesis Games. I think I'll be taking a break from this series for awhile since the quality is so inconsistent.

title: The Winter of Our Discontent
author: John Steinbeck
review:
This was my least favorite Steinbeck novel so far. The theme of the novel has a lot of potential but the execution is a bit shoddy and most of the moral ambiguity is dealt with in the last third of the book without much build up and a lot of things sort of happen "off-camera" with multiple time skips that leave the reader puzzled about what happened.

What's disappointing about this novel is I didn't feel connected to any of the characters the way that I have in other Steinbeck novels. Ethan Allen Hawley's motivations are subtle and unclear most of the time as are Margie's as his feminine foil. The contrast between Ethan and Samuel in East of Eden is quite stark where even though Samuel was not present in most of Eden, the reader understands him deeply and feels the ripples of his influence throughout the novel. In The Winter of Out Discontent Ethan does not have that same effect and neither do the supporting characters as they do in Cannery Row which makes this novel overall disappointing.

title: Nausea
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
review:
Nausea is an introspective, lonely look into a life where a man starts to question the meaning of things around him and morosely views his past and contemplates revisiting a once long term relationship that ended slowly and quietly. It isn't a good feeling to relate to the book, but in some ways I think we all do. I read Camus' The Stranger a while ago and think that book overall will stick with me more than Nausea, but Nausea does arrive at an interesting point in my life where it's easy to relate to the character and their situation which makes it more relatable and induces more thought. There are some stretches of the book that aren't as consistently interesting and more mundane parts of the main character's life, but I guess it all can't be a morose slog through a lonely miserable
existential existence. So it is odd how the book does feel longer than it is, probably due to the heavy subject matter, but there also a few tangents that I found didn't add to my overall experience of the novel.

title: Gardens of the Moon
author: Steven Erikson
review:
Never read anything quite like this book. This is an incredibly dense fantasy novel and I have been warned about this multiple times both in person and online that this can be difficult to get through.

I actually found the writing to be "fast" to read and enjoyed Erikson's style of shorter POV sections that hop to different characters at interesting points in their stories, I never felt like it was dragging at all, but quite the opposite where sometimes it's challenging to keep up. The difficult part of the book in my mind is the number of characters, the mechanics of the world, and the emerging politics. This is truly a window to another world which is tonally different than an author like Brandon Sanderson, nothing will be explained to you; you have to absorb it from the world and the interactions of the characters.

Succeeding at reading this book is accepting that you won't know everything and recognizing that events happened even though you might not understand how or why that event happened. I struggled the most during action scenes with the magic mechanics, I don't really understand how Warrens work yet and had to slowly read through the action scenes to not miss anything. They do take unexpected turns than simply action scenes with sword fights and the world is so different than our own that the outcomes are quite different than what you expect which can be challenging, but also is engaging.

My worry going forward with the series is the amount of Deus Ex Machina in the plot, there were a few times where a character would be saved by other characters that I either couldn't remember were in close proximity or swooped in at the last second that was a little unrealistic. Warrens also as a plot device makes me concerned, because it's effectively teleporting and I don't understand the limits to this or if there are any. Magic systems in general make me skeptical of the plot, but it will be interesting to see if this can be refined in later entries in the series.

title: Deadhouse Gates
author: Steven Erikson
review:
Exponentially better than the first book, I immediately got hooked and devoured this book a lot faster than I expected despite its length. Erikson really has come into his own in this entry and the character development is a lot stronger here than Gardens of the Moon by removing some of the complexity and trimming down the number of parallel storylines to a more manageable number you are able to build better connections to the characters and the storylines often overlap and then diverge again which is exciting and unexpected in many ways.

I am a huge fan of the structure of the book and the way Erikson changes point of view, you always seem to get enough time with your favorite characters and the transition points are often satisfying where you're not waiting long periods of time to figure out what happened to them after ending on a cliffhanger. You're provided with enough information to form theories in your head of where their story might go, but also left at good stopping points for their characters.

There's a few fantastic twists in this entry that are frankly jaw-dropping and unexpected and subvert fantasy tropes.

The way the world is described and the events that unfold color the story in such a way that you really feel like you are there with these characters in a beautiful, brutal, and horrifying world. There's so many instances where the contrast of the beauty and horror often are orchestrated in the same setting, it's truly masterful storytelling and pushes you forward to continue reading and learn more about this world. The complexity of the world is astounding, but the way it is threaded by Erikson builds trust in the author that even if something is confusing or mysterious it's meant to be that way for now and might become clearer later on in the series. Most major events are comprehensible although there is usually some aspect of things that may not be completely clear but don't distract enough to damper the overarching narrative.

I complained about the Deus Ex Machina of the last entry and in this one it's gotten better, but not completely fixed. In some ways it seems you have to accept the magic and the gods as a reality of this universe and that means that characters can be saved in their time of need or travel large distances quickly. I don't think this was as jarring as in Gardens of the Moon; you often accompany these characters when they are traveling in warrens so it does help paint a better picture of how these systems work. The warrens and magic are often mysterious and not even completely understood by the characters using them, which is fascinating as well.

title: Memories of Ice
author: Steven Erikson
review:
**spoiler alert** Overall I enjoyed Deadhouse Gates more, but this entry has more of a traditional epic fantasy feel that puts its own spin on it. I don't want to understate the epic scale of this book however, the siege battle of Capustan was incredible and visceral and the ending stretch of the battle of Coral is one of my favorite stretches of 200 or so pages of the whole series so far and is simply jaw dropping in the increasing stakes and sheer scale.

I was expecting more main character deaths in this entry just based on things I had heard about online, Whiskeyjack's death is major and he was definitely more fleshed out in this entry and his death is truly tragic, however was expecting even more fallout from the battle of Coral.

I enjoyed the overall theme of forgiveness in this book and can't overstate how unique this is. This is personified by Itkovian, but a lot of the characters struggle with finding their place in the world in this entry and their redemption is often in forgiving their enemies. The theme of this entry really makes the world richer and the moral complexity going forward much higher.

There was enough cryptic magical happenings that put a slight damper on it for me that I think Deadhouse Gates managed better; there were a lot of dream sequences and teleportation that aren't really explained that put this below DG for me.

Silverfox's arc really fell short for me, was expecting her to be a more central character in this book and it kind of just fizzled out. Maybe that was the point, but wasn't expecting her to refuse to lift the curse from the T'lan Imass, however it was confusing how she waffled on this but then they decide to go south to save some of their kin. Just overall somewhat of a confusing and unsatisfying story arc on Silverfox's side.

Really enjoyed the storyline with Lady Envy, Tool, and Toc, the group of traveling companions just had really interesting dialogue and chemistry; Tool is one of the most unexpected favorite characters as a seemingly unfeeling undead character that eventually it's apparent has more and more of a personality.

I really loved Itkovian's arc as a character, at first I wasn't really sure how he connected with the rest of the story and was just a generic soldier in Capustan. During the siege battle, his interaction with Gruntle, and his identity crisis with Fener entering the mortal realm was well articulated and gave the character a lot of depth. I hope this trend continues and Erikson continues to build rich characters like this.

On the flipside, I didn't feel a lot of connection to many of the Bridgeburners. Picker is only the real one that stands out to me, maybe Spindle as well, but they don't have fully formed personalities in my mind and are somewhat interchangeable. I felt a lot closer to the newer characters than the Bridgeburners.

Things I'm unsure about after reading:

- Why the love for Itkovian from other soldiers? Didn't he effectively prevent the T'lan Imass from fighting the K'Chain Che'Malle and thus cause a lot of excess casualties from Dujek's army?
- How did Tool turn back into a human at the end of the book? Was this from Itkovian taking the burden of the T'lan Imass? I'm still unsure what taking their burden means, I thought they'd disappear into dust like earlier in the book.
- I'm generally confused about Toc the Younger's ending arc, I'm not sure why he needed to change bodies and killed himself at the end of the book and his real connection to the wolf god. Overall confused of all the rules in this universe about rebirth and seems somewhat inconsistent compared to how Tattersail's rebirth was handled.

title: How to Lie with Maps
author: Mark Monmonier
review: In a word: antiquated. Even with the allegedly updated third edition of the book, most of the examples are about drawing maps with pen and paper, something that isn't done often in this day and age. The examples of lying with maps are also often pretty elementary -- such as a map maker adding places that don't exist or low resolution satellite images. Not very compelling to read about and there aren't good strategies mentioned for mitigating these "lies". There are some interesting thoughts on feature selection in the book and what information to convey to readers that save this book from being a waste of time, however they are pretty few and far between.

title: House of Chains
author: Steven Erikson
review:
**spoiler alert** Although I rated this a 3/5 and Gardens of the Moon a 4/5, I liked this entry more than the first, but my expectations have been adjusted as I've gotten deeper into the series.

Things I liked about this entry:

- Karsa Orlong: I enjoyed the focus on this character in the beginning and his overall arc in this entry. Having more time with a subset of the characters is why I liked Deadhouse Gates so much and the story is the strongest and most coherent when we're not constantly jumping around (although there is probably the most jumping around since Gardens in the second half of the book). Icarium vs Karsa was probably my favorite part of the book and made me really nervous since I'm a big fan of them both (and Mappo of course), I hope the series continues to have main characters at odds with each other. If anything, this novel could have been more aggressive with that, there seemed to be some pretty obvious baddies here on Shaik's side with Korbolo Dom and Bidithal, would be more interesting to have main characters be on opposite sides with a more dedicated view that their side is right.
- Theme and imagery: Just really strong images of chains and the thematic cohesion around slavery in society and to gods was really great here. I like this trend that Erikson has of making each entry thematically distinct while also adding little nuggets here and there of ice, dust, etc that you can guess are the thematic core of future entries based on their titles.
- Heboric: I'm really interested in the development in his character, and his dream / trip with the tea was one of my favorite parts of the series and seemed to really pull back the curtain on some of the larger conflicts going on in the series. Heboric just seems like a very flawed character but inherently good with an interesting background that makes for developments surrounding him to be unexpected.
- Larger scope: It's interesting that this series starts with a very narrow scope; a single character who is naive of the larger world, its history, and even themselves and then explodes into a multi-realm power struggle. Erikson comes close to tipping his hand here where you can see some of the larger threads of the story connecting between gods. I get the feeling that Osric, Cotillion, and some other gods that are alluded to will become bigger players in future entries.

Things I'm indifferent to:

- Crokus and Apsalar: Had potential, but kind of fell flat, not sure where they are really going and some of their time together wasn't that interesting, but I did like their interactions with Cotillion even though I don't really buy their relationship to him. Shouldn't Apsalar hate Cotillion? Especially after he possessed her and destroyed her whole fishing village?
- Shaik vs Tavore: Felt pretty anticlimactic after everything after the first book onward foreshadows the clash between them only to have it end so quickly and no real character developments follow from it. Felisin elder felt kind of wasted here, she didn't have many meaningful decisions to make and didn't seem to particularly take a stance about why the Malazan empire was evil.

Things I didn't like:

- Trull Sengar and Onrack: Just not very invested in this storyline and it wasn't particularly interesting. Hopefully the development of these characters continues more throughout the series to make sense of their appearance here. Was just pretty bored with their adventures in this one.
- Pearl and Lostara: Felt like a pretty pointless side quest here and wasted potential. Might have accomplished some world building, but I would have been fine with this being left out of the book. I was hoping for some interaction between Pearl and Kalam after their encounter in Deadhouse Gates.

title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
review:
**spoiler alert** Despite having read 1984 around 3 times previously for some reason I hadn't read Animal Farm until now. I definitely wasn't expecting it to be quite so similar to 1984 and so bleak. Boxer's story of being a hardworking idealistic workhorse that is looking forward to retirement and sent to the glue factory is all too relevant in present day as well despite being written in 1945.

It's an easy read, but the themes of the book definitely hit you by the end of the novel and the hope for society is greatly diminished after reading. As is the seemingly inevitable erosion of rights by the ruling class that rules absolutely as we go from "Four legs good! Two legs bad!" to the haunting image of the pigs learning to walk on two legs and being indistinguishable from men. "The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig; but already it was impossible to say which was which". I think I'll need a pick me up after this one.

title: Midnight Tides
author: Steven Erikson
review:
**spoiler alert** My ranking of the series so far from best to worst:

- Deadhouse Gates
- Memories of Ice
- Midnight Tides
- House of Chains
- Gardens of the Moon

I was really concerned about this entry starting out, it's really bold and unnerving for Erikson to again change the location and introduce mostly all new characters. However, this is one of the most self contained stories in this series so far and echoes similar to what I enjoyed about Deadhouse Gates so much, tight storylines that eventually converge.

This series is really challenging with how much it alternates from the best thing I've ever read to incoherent magical drivel, I'm not sold on the magic system or the gods yet and my favorite parts of the series almost always do not involve magic or the gods.

Things I liked about this entry:

- Trull Sengar: Wow, what a turnaround for a character, from pretty uneventful and boring in the last book to a deep character in Midnight Tides. The journey to recover the sword was where I started getting engaged with the book at around the 200 page mark, just a beautifully described passage of Trull fending off the Jheck and then Rhulad getting resurrected was very unexpected and disturbing.
- Tehol and Bugg: Ok, I had no idea this series could be this funny. Their banter was just amazing and bizarre. From Tehol's uneven trousers to Bugg seducing a woman with a dead fish on a date, these guys have it all. Bugg being Mael was an interesting reveal, I don't really get all the implications, but seemed fitting and was hinted at that while they appear to be foolish characters they also outwit everyone they encounter and have knowledge about things that most people in the world do not.
- Lilac: The sympathetic demons are some of my favorite characters in these books. Trull saving Lilac and sending him back to his realm was incredibly heartwarming, I'm assuming we'll see him in the future since he's soulbound to Trull.
- Brother dynamics: I felt that the symmetry in this book was pretty astounding, Erikson really plays off the two sets of brothers from the Edur in the Sengars and Letherii in the Beddicts and sort of turns it on its head with having some of the Beddicts embedded with the Edur with varying motivations. Erikson kind of cheats and gets some character backstory "for free" by having them be brothers from the same family but I really enjoyed having this relationship between the characters and it gave them a lot of depth, Fear Sengar in particular.
- The battle of Letheras (Battle of Brans Keep): Hannan Mosag just unleashing a huge amount of sorcery on the Letherii soldiers was disturbing and grandiose, especially since it wiped out thousands of their own troops.

Things I'm confused about / didn't like:

- The Champion that pulled up Brys Beddict at the ending seemingly appeared out of nowhere and I didn't remember him appearing earlier in the book, just seemed like a random event that I felt wasn't explained well.
- Udinaas: Him being possesed by the Wyval and its motivations just seemed very ill explained. I enjoyed Udinaas' role as Rhulad's Eunuch, but his end of the book just wasn't explained very well. Also by extension, Feather Witch's part of the story was disjointed as well, not the strongest parts of the book.
- Rhulad's ascension to the throne: The scene of him taking power seemed unbelievable to me. I'm not sure why no-one would contest this, Rhulad didn't seem particularly powerful even if he was immortal, he wasn't a particularly good fighter even after having the power of the Crippled God.

title: The Last Wish
author: Andrzej Sapkowski
review:
**spoiler alert** After getting through 5 books in the Malazan series, I needed a more character focused fantasy read. With the Witcher show about to premiere on Netflix and having played the Witcher 3, thought I would give this a read. Overall I enjoyed my time and plan on continuing the series, but this entry was far from perfect.

Wasn't a big fan of the short story format of the book, it didn't ruin it by any stretch, but it made the narrative less cohesive and some of the stories didn't build Geralt or the world beyond being an interesting monster hunt.

I thought that there would be more to the beginning of Geralt and Yennefer's relationship and it didn't really make a whole lot of sense why he was drawn to her even though she did actively betray him, maybe this will make more sense in future books.

title: The Bonehunters
author: Steven Erikson
review:
Steven Erikson is a mad genius. My favorite entry yet, possibly one of the best books I've ever read. Characters that you've grown with over the series all come together in surprising and sometimes heartbreaking ways. Convergence with a capital "C", I'm awestruck by how well things came together and the foresight that Erikson had to set up some of the dominoes that he's begun to knock over.

And there's a sense that the best is yet to come. Hyped.

title: Everything Is F*cked: A Book About Hope
author: Mark Manson

title: Reaper's Gale
author: Steven Erikson
review:
**spoiler alert** Much slower start than The Bonehunters, but the emotional weight and stakes of the story increases substantially in this entry and the payoff at the end is incredible. However, I do wonder if some of the traveling and sub-plots could have been shortened to make getting to the "good stuff" faster.

Some of the most heart-wrenching moments of the series yet, the death of major characters was pretty surprising but pulled off in ways that made sense. Particularly the deaths of Toc and Trull hit me the hardest, which isn't to say that Beak's death wasn't majorly impactful as well.

Redmask

I thought Redmask's story was compelling but didn't have much of the emotional weight of the other storylines aside from, of course, Toc the Younger. I have mixed feelings about his battle failing due to a mistimed cavalry charge and am confused about why the K'Chain Che'malle turned on him (just because he was losing the battle?). Toc has to be one of the most unlucky people in the Malazan universe. Also, Tool arriving just after his best friend died is so depressing.

Beak

Erikson flexes his short story writing skills with Beak in this book, a truly tragic character with a heart of gold that ends up saving his friends and dying in the process. I could see his death coming, but it was really well written and him meeting up with his brother in the afterlife is bittersweet.

Icarium and Tarlack Veed, Karsa

This story line in Lether really dragged in the first 3/4 of the book and wish a lot more had been cut. Karsa, Icarium, and Tarlack Veed didn't have a whole lot to do in Letheras for most of the book. Karsa fighting Rhulad towards the end of the book was exciting and awesome, but Erikson really teased us with this fight for a bit too long. I'm still trying to make sense of what happened to Icarium, maybe it will be explained better later in the series. I actually grew more sympathetic to Tarlack in this book, I don't think he's a bad person, he's in a tough spot and his death scene was tragic with him picturing his home town and his old life. Working for the Nameless Ones seems like a no-win scenario for anyone and I could see him becoming as sympathetic as Mappo given time.

Silchas Ruin and co

This storyline did feel like it dragged a bit, but I did enjoy the dynamics of the traveling group and it gave some contrast to the bromances that Erikson sprinkles in regularly with a group that has major reservations about eachother and in the end fights to the death. The moral complexity with Silchas Ruin is interesting, I'm still not sure if he is truly a villain or not and the story of Scabandari and whether Blood Eye was totally in the wrong or if Silchas Ruin was always a bit of a bastard.

The parallel of Fear Sengar about to stab Silchas in the back was well done, that scene with the convergence of Trull, Fear, Silchas and company was hair raising and made me fear for all the characters that I've grown close to.

Quick Ben

What a badass, we see Quick Ben's true power here. Him blasting Silchas Ruin with Fiddler was so awesome as was his quip "Fucking dragon". Unexpected, because in a traditional fantasy book we'd probably see Silchas Ruin be a big villain with a harder fight, but Steven Erikson subverts expectations yet again (although this is similar to what he did with Raest in Garden's of the Moon).

Fiddler and the Bonehunters

Nothing too far from the norm from Fiddler which is good, but we did get to see the marines in action and see Fiddler show the boys how it's done and set bombs like the best of them. The demon farmers was a highlight and just really painted their whole campaign gray especially after we interacted with demons with hearts of gold with Trull in Midnight Tides, it seemed like they just wanted to settle down but were dragged into this conflict.

Feather Witch and the Errant

I guess Feather Witch is a full fledged baddie now, her eating the eye of the Errant was a great scene. However, I in general have a hard time keeping context of Feather Witch's state of mind in the series especially since it can be awhile between times that we catch up with her, especially since Midnight Tides, so I'll have to go back and see what happened where she got so extreme in her beliefs.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
author: Kurt Vonnegut Jr.
review: Read this initially in high school as "required" reading and loved it. Revisiting this years later and it still holds up. This the ultimate distilled Vonnegut novel and the story flows easily between chapters. Great introduction to the Vonnegut literary universe.

title: The Old Man and the Sea
author: Ernest Hemingway

title: The Blade Itself
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
Character focused fantasy that feels like a living, breathing world. I feel like other reviews focus too much on how this is "grimdark" when it doesn't feel dark for the sake of being dark, but because that's the way this world is and it has moments of beauty and splendor and it has moments of darkness and violence.

Abercrombie balances the tightrope between a gritty realistic world and comedy with mastery, often you are laughing one minute and then on the edge of your seat the next. The comedy never cheapens the payoffs of characters or plot events.

My only criticism of this would only be that this novel is mostly setup of what I'm assuming are longer arcs, but the setup feels great. It never feels like you're in a rush to get somewhere like other fantasy novels and you get to soak in the atmosphere of the world. However you lose some of what epic fantasy offers with global moving pieces and it's all a bit of a blur at the macroscopic level, but the relationships between characters is crystal clear, ever evolving, and intriguing.

title: Before They Are Hanged
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
Doesn't deliver on the promise of the first novel and there's some character development that seemed somewhat unearned and a little jarring. Biggest gripe is that many of the characters don't have that much of an impact on the overarching plot so it can seem fairly anticlimactic and the world building continues to not be a focus. The main villains are also not too fleshed out and a little generic.

It is a little puzzling that this series is compared to a Song of Ice and Fire when it doesn't come close to the highs of that series so far. That being said, I do enjoy the moment to moment reading of the series and a lot of the characters are fantastic. Hoping that further entries payoff from this slightly awkward middle book.

title: Last Argument of Kings
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
Liked it, didn't love it. More like 3.75 stars than 3. Things from the last book make more sense now and are more or less wrapped up thankfully. The ending was somewhat overly long and overstayed its welcome a bit, could have been a bit tighter wrapping things up, didn't have to know every last detail of how things ended up for the B and C plots.

This series is a bit overhyped in my opinion, had a lot more enjoyment from a Song of Ice and Fire and Malazan at their highs than this series. I did enjoy my time with some of the characters, world building here was not too great and the political intrigue leaves a lot to be desired.

title: The Lies of Locke Lamora
author: Scott Lynch
review: Who doesn't love a heist? Perfectly put together story that keeps you guessing and caring about the characters. The audiobook narration is perfection; Michael Page's inflection of characters pretending to be other characters has to be heard to be believed. Just on a completely otherworldly level narration-wise. Also, the story is self contained even though this is a series, so you don't feel obligated to keep going and can take a break.

title: Death Masks
author: Jim Butcher
review:
Hells bells. When will you grow up, Harry Dresden? Really no character development to be seen 5 books in and just way too cheesy for my taste. The chauvinism in this entry seems particularly noticeable as well and just lots of cringey moments sprinkled throughout.

Think I'm done with this series; they seem to keep treading the same ground and aren't pushing me to keep going. Dresden can be a bit of a dumbass a lot of times and can be difficult to root for.

title: Assassin's Quest
author: Robin Hobb
review:
August 2025:
Still an amazing read. Knowing the full story makes me appreciate everything Hobb set up here that pays off in later books.

July 2020:
Robin Hobb makes you care about her characters so much that it hurts a little bit. The way she writes just completely transports my mind into her world; it's wonderful. Fitz gets metaphorically and sometimes literally kicked in the balls repeatedly but he endures. This entry changes up from the previous two in the titular 'quest' fashion, it's a peek from the peephole of Fitz's perspective to a larger world and is refreshing. There is a bit of bloat in this entry and could have been condensed some, but honestly it's nice to spend time with these characters even if they're doing mundane things such as setting up camp or surviving in the wilderness. I ravenously consumed this one and still want more.

title: The Way of Kings
author: Brandon Sanderson
review:
It seems like I'm one of the few that isn't in love with this book, I enjoyed it but didn't think it was a revelation by any stretch. Interestingly, Sanderson seems to gravitate towards classic fantasy tropes in this book and mostly eschews modern fantasy trends.

I didn't think the budget in terms of page count was used in the way I usually look for in books. This is a massive book! I expect a lot to happen with a page count like this and major events to occur. The characters don't tend to change a whole lot from the beginning of the novel (or at least past the 10% mark) to at least the 85% mark and the pages mainly are involved with exploring the history of the world or flashback sequences for the characters. I'm personally not a huge fan of flashbacks / visions unless used sparingly, they were done well here and were interesting, but a large portion of the book is taken up by them.

I'm also not completely immersed in the world, it doesn't feel quite "real" to me yet. The ideas are interesting and the fauna and weather are interesting but it doesn't seem to permeate society in the way that I'd expect. I also cringe a little bit whenever someone says "Storm off!".

All that being said, I'm continuing on with Words of Radiance and hoping the world and narrative grabs me more. For what it's worth the prose is pretty strong and understated, I also got really invested in some of the characters and they're all fairly interesting even though they didn't grow as much as I'd like.

title: Ship of Destiny
author: Robin Hobb
review:
The trilogy transcends the Fantasy genre and is elevated to one of the finest literary trilogies of all time in my mind. Hobb tackles weighty topics fundamental to the core of what it means to be human and challenges the reader to think deeply about a number of timeless issues (slavery, family honor, coming of age).

She builds multifaceted characters like none other that force the reader to be invested and care about her characters as people and not as fictional beings. It's honestly astounding the amount these characters go through and how much they change throughout this trilogy.

Hobb has architected an epic narrative with a large cast of characters that all fit together and evolve in a way that makes sense. The events of this trilogy have huge implications for her sprawling world and the larger series.

title: Words of Radiance
author: Brandon Sanderson
review: I can definitively say that Brandon Sanderson is not for me.

title: Fool's Errand
author: Robin Hobb
review:
You can't go home again. However, we go back to Fitz in this book and it feels an awful lot like home. It's good to be back with Fitz after being away from him on the Liveship trilogy. This book hits a lot of classic fantasy notes but the execution here is exemplary; showing that you don't have to always do an edgy modern take to have a story with impact.

Hobb's prose is flowery while being as precise as a surgeon's knife. She always has the perfect word to describe something and paint the scene. I'll never get tired of her descriptions of her characters eating an extravagant meal or setting up camp. It always feels visceral and real. She brings us into the world of the Six Duchies in what seems like an effortless stroke of her pen.

Under a less masterful writer this story would be tedious, under Hobb it is transcendent.

title: Golden Fool
author: Robin Hobb
review:
Very much a transitionary entry that wraps up some events in the first book and sets up the conflict for the final book in the trilogy.

Has some hard hitting moments, but definitely suffers from middle book syndrome. However, I've grown to trust Hobb to lay the foundation that will eventually pay off. This book is a lot of foundation building of things that are bound to be epic in the next book.

title: The Dragon Keeper
author: Robin Hobb
review: Definitely Hobb's weakest book by a longshot. Still decent to read, but she isn't true to the form we've come to expect in previous books. Returning characters are also woefully underutilized and we end up spending most of our time with new characters which is a bit disappointing, was hoping that we would get more time with the characters from the Liveship trilogy and build on them. Also the book sort of...just ends? Not a satisfying conclusion or self-contained story, makes more sense when you finish the second one.

title: Dragon Haven
author: Robin Hobb
review:
3.5/5 Better than the first book. Hobb *heavily* uses romantic relationships in this series as a device to tackle issues such as society, co-evolution of the Rainwilders and dragons, coming of age, and tradition vs making your own rules. Usually the romantic relationships are central to the plot which is a stark contrast to her other works.

I could see this making it challenging to read or not fitting most reader's tastes, although I think it worked pretty well and the romances are usually in the context of building a new society, thinking about the construct of marriage, and even LGBTQ relationships and the ethics involved there. It was close to being overly fetishized, but to me it didn't cross any barriers there and was still tastefully done. It felt like these relationships were used in an effective way to provide thinking points for the reader, but is a stark contrast to her other books where romance was used sparingly.

Her prose is surprisingly less pronounced in these novels, but there is a distinct survival theme in this book that is interesting and provides more color to her world. Overall, I liked it but I definitely don't think it's at the bar of her other books, although it is enjoyable and does provide things to think about.

title: City of Dragons
author: Robin Hobb
review: Hobb trims a lot of the fat here and the novel is more concise while still having a lot happening. Characters in the Liveship trilogy have more to do here and have an interesting role in the overarching story.

title: Blood of Dragons
author: Robin Hobb
review:
Pretty solid quadrilogy, however doesn't have the impact of Hobb's other series. Has some really interesting world building and major events the impact the world writ large in this series, so by no means is this skippable in the larger Realm of the Elderlings books without missing out.

The characters in this series end up being fairly interesting, but we don't reach the depths of her other books unfortunately, so while this is a decent series by any other standard, it's the weakest of Hobb's.

The characterization of the dragons, however, is excellent and probably the strongest part of the series as is delving more into the complicated history of the Elderlings.

This series definitely leans more closely to YA than her other books simply due to the age of a lot of her characters which can get a bit tiring, but she does explore interesting ideas using romance as a plot device so I didn't find it as grating as other readers seemed to.

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
review:
This book is undoubtedly a classic and I really loved it the first time I read it in high school. Right now I think it's a fairly solid book, but I think what really brought it over the edge for my in previous reads was Dune Messiah and Children of Dune rounding out the setup in Dune proper. On its own there's some stumbles along the way, especially in the beginning of the book, things are very slow to get started. Also the ending just sort of happens and some major events happen offscreen which is a little disappointing. From what I remember, the story seems more complete after the second and third books where Herbert's pessimistic sirens against organized religion and politics hits full blast.

What's exceptional about this book however is the theme of prophecy and visions as seen through Paul. There is an inevitable march towards disaster that no character can seem to derail and Herbert tackles topics such as religion, politics, and socio-economics through a critical lens. I definitely appreciated this book on the first read more than this read, now that I've read more science fiction and fantasy this one seems less groundbreaking, but given the time period this was written in it's foundational to a huge swath of SFF, and you can see its influences in a lot of speculative fiction that's currently being written.

title: Best Served Cold
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
4.5/5

This is my favorite Abercrombie book so far. He excels when the stories are smaller and the stakes are lower. The First Law trilogy really struggled trying to fill the boots of epic fantasy, this one doesn't try to do that and it results in a better story that's more focused in what it wants to accomplish.

The dialogue in this book is amazing and sharply written, there's a lot of laugh out loud moments and the characters jump out of the page and are well defined. You can often tell what character is talking based on just how they're talking which is really impressive. The characters are really well developed and complex here, the world is very gray and often completely black where everyone is sort of awful all the time, but there are some moments of friendship; before they turn around and try to kill each-other that is.

This is one of the best audiobooks I've ever listened to. Steven Pacey deserves heaps of praise, every character sounds unique and he brings the story to life as a play performed by one man. I have no idea how he pulls it off but he often goes from one character to another mid-breath and even in certain moments has characters pretending to be other characters...just amazing.

title: Malice
author: John Gwynne
review:
Malice is an adrenaline shot straight to the heart of the modern Fantasy genre; things happen in Malice and they happen fast. If you're tired of lots of filler and events taking a long time to happen in the Fantasy books you're reading Malice is the antidote to that fatigue.

Gwynne time skips aggressively to get past the boring parts and get right to the good stuff, and it works well. He's playing a balancing act here and it's artfully pulled off where he risks making the story confusing or rushed, but it never feels that way. You can tell that he's confident in his ability to pull off the story and he does so. My biggest concern going forward is if he's used up most of the twist and turns for the first book because it moves so fast, but we will see.

The story is fairly standard good vs evil at the surface level but there is a lot of mystery in the mythology and politics of the world where things are not quite as they seem. Gwynne uses prophecy here excellently to move the plot forward and make the motivations of the characters complex.

The characters are well done and have a surprising amount of depth given how fast the plot moves. This book is purposely eschewing grimdark trends in modern Fantasy and it's refreshing to have characters that you can actually root for, are intrinsically good, and care about their family and friends; it makes their losses matter and their triumphs sweeter. This is more in the vein of classic Fantasy, but Gwynne has a modern take on it.

My favorite part about Gwynne so far is that it feels like he values your time and is very efficient with the page count of this book. Enough happens in this book to have been a trilogy in the hands of other authors but he maintains the delicate act of hitting you with well-developed characters and not losing you in the details.

title: Hyperion
author: Dan Simmons
review:
The humanity shines through despite this being in the far future and a world apart from where we are now. It does this in a realistic way, humans still act similar to how they do today but with access to a swathe of futuristic technology that is indistinguishable from magic. The characters are more well done than a lot of other science fiction stories; Simmons is able to portray his vision for the future in multiple distinct perspectives. The structure of this story is really well done and the memoir-like chapters take very unexpected turns and connect to each-other in interesting ways so there's a ton of variety here.

Something that really stood out to me are the elements of horror in the book, the Shrike is very spooky and mysterious, so you also get elements of a great horror novel intermixed with the memoir and sci-fi elements that are wholly unique.

It's also interesting how prominent the alien worlds' fauna and creatures are. The atmosphere of these worlds are all different and dangerous despite how advanced the technology is, our characters can come to harm from the natural forces as well.

My biggest knock against this is it feels like half the book is missing and just ends abruptly, but planning on reading the next book immediately to hopefully get a satisfying conclusion.

title: Assassin's Fate
author: Robin Hobb
review: Thank you Robin Hobb for writing these books. This is the best series I have ever read.

title: Ruin
author: John Gwynne
review:
This book is absolutely epic in every way, the number of POVs has increased steadily from the first book and you get to see all sides of the conflict in interesting ways. There's some great character moments that have been building throughout the series and finally pay off here and some twists that you don't see coming.

This one has one of the best duels I've ever read and multiple large scale battles that are all distinct from one-another, Gwynne does action sequences exceptionally well and they're easy to visualize what exactly is going on.

title: The Fall of Hyperion
author: Dan Simmons
review:
The scale of this book is pretty huge which is both a pro and a con to this entry, you lose some of the intimacy with the first book and the stakes get raised massively in the second part of this story. The themes in this book regarding environmentalism, technology, and human nature are extremely poignant and relevant to this day. It's pretty mind-blowing that Simmons wrote this before the internet surged in popularity and scale, a lot that's in this book could be seen as commentary on today's world of instant communication and technological intrusion into our daily lives.

The book isn't perfect and I think some of the characterization that was done so well in the first book sort of suffers here, but it's done at the expense of telling a huge, universe-impacting story so it makes sense why this is the case. One other thing I would add is that the line between futuristic technology and magic here becomes very blurred and the mysticism of this book can be a bit heavy, but it's usually done to serve an analysis on religion and human nature. The world feels very real and impossibly plausible for how the future might look like which is a huge accomplishment given just how advanced this future society is.

title: Red Rising
author: Pierce Brown
review: I really enjoyed this one and blew through it in a few days. The reviews that mention that this is a blend of Hunger Games, Ender's Game, and Lord of the Flies are spot on. There's also an interesting blend of class warfare in here too, and some pretty great twists that keep you guessing. It stays fresh throughout and there's a major revelation / turn that mixes up the dynamics of the book every few chapters that pushes you forward, wanting to know what happens. The story can be pretty dark too, which I love. No one is safe!

title: Morning Star
author: Pierce Brown
review:
I was beginning to get a little burnt out on this series towards the end, there's probably more padding in this book than the other two books. Although the ending is really well done and some of the twists and betrayals are pretty great. This book always tries to be a little bit deeper than just a fun action romp, it's partially successful, but there's some descriptions and themes that pull me out of it a little bit since they're not executed quite as well as they could be.

I will probably pick up the follow up trilogy once that's completed, the world is interesting and there's enough fallout *cough* to deal with after the events of the finale that I will be curious to see how they're handled in the next set of books.

title: One Piece, Volume 2: Buggy the Clown
author: Eiichiro Oda

title: The Shadow of the Torturer
author: Gene Wolfe
review:
If there's one thing to say about The Shadow of the Torturer, it's that it is unique and also challenges the reader profusely. Although it's barely over 200 pages, it demands a lot of thought from the reader untying the Gordian Knot that is the narrative where you feel like you are immersed in a three dimensional alien puzzle where you don't know the rules and you don't even have all the pieces yet.

Reading this book is like accidentally stumbling into the dreams of another person that is barely keeping their sanity intact.

The plot is distinctly non-linear and postmodern in many ways and will not hold your hand or explain what is happening for better or worse. The benefits of this are that you are immediately immersed in Severian's head and his working knowledge of the world around him.

This work is also extremely metatextual, allegorical, and metaphorical from a wide variety of cultures, religions, and languages. This makes the text incredibly rich and dense which also makes the book feel a lot longer than it actually is, because you can read a single sentence and extract multiple meanings from it. Likely this means that every person reading it will get something unique from it, which is not easy to do by any means. Gene Wolfe does have passages in this book where he nods to the reader and sort of breaks the fourth wall, at one point even telling you that he understands if you don't continue reading Severian's journey.

That being said there is an actual plot which can be understood in the reality this takes place in, although it's certainly fair to say that you will not have a clear picture of how this world works or that Severian will actively tell you conflicting information in which you need to decide for yourself what is this novel's reality and which is distorted from his perspective on events. In effect, this means that the world will feel "fuzzy" or cloudy and you won't have a full picture of the rules of the world or what's even possible in this world by the end of the book.

The more I think about this book the more that I like it. However, it'll most likely depend on how the series develops and if things actually start making sense or not. I could see myself finishing the series and looking back on this book as a piece of genius or as an impenetrable mess. Or possibly get frustrated and not finish the whole thing. At this point all the outcomes seem equally likely.

title: The Dragonbone Chair
author: Tad Williams
review:
March 2023 Re-read in preparation for reading Last King of Osten Ard for the first time.

One of my favorite first books of a series, up there with Fellowship of the Ring in terms of coziness especially the first part of the book is so soothing and nice.

Tad does an incredible job with the world building and introducing a world with a huge amount of history and lore.

Although I love this book I do think it has some fairly obvious flaws and doesn't introduce the politics and make you care as much as A Song of Ice and Fire does, where some of the storylines have a bit awkward beginnings here and you wonder why they're there. These were a bit better on a re-read but I still think this could have been done a bit better.

Tad also is definitely overlong and that's definitely his biggest flaw. However the prose is absolutely gorgeous and there's some sections of the book that are incredibly beautiful, deep, and profound. His foreshadowing is also really good and makes a re-read really interesting to examine what he told you and when.

Osten Ard is one of my favorite fantasy worlds and I'm grateful to spend more time in it, really excited for the sequel series and to see how things have changed and what's next in the series.

title: One Piece, Volume 3: Don't Get Fooled Again
author: Eiichiro Oda

title: Stone of Farewell
author: Tad Williams
review:
Re-read. Definitely a middle book but a lot more happens than I remember. There's an overarching theme of "these characters need to move from where they're not supposed to be to where they are supposed to be" but actually a lot more happens than I remembered. The world of Osten Ard can be a dangerous and scary place, especially when larger events are causing the world to become undone.

I'm very excited for the conclusion and there's a lot of climactic moments that I remember that I'm interested in re-experiencing. One of my favorite series and have been very happy with my decision to re-read before the last book comes out in November.

title: To Green Angel Tower
author: Tad Williams
review:
Re-reading this series was an absolute treat. My favorite classical fantasy series just behind Lord of the Rings. Very excited to read the sequel series very soon.

A lot of great scenes in this book and it uses the page count well even though it's one of the largest fantasy books written. Love the immersion and moments of horror Tad has in his stories.

title: The Sword of the Lictor
author: Gene Wolfe
series: The Book of the New Sun, #3

title: Sharp Ends
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
Liked this one more than I expected to. Abercrombie just has fun with this one, the dialogue is great and hilarious and he fleshes out some of the gaps from his previous stories.

Would highly recommend *not* reading this unless you have read all of the preceding novels since some of the stories won't make sense unless you have read them.

title: Invincible, Vol. 2: Eight Is Enough
author: Robert Kirkman
review: Starting to get interesting, still a little meh so far. Seems like it's taking a bit to get started, so far not too different from a generic superhero story.

title: A Time of Dread
author: John Gwynne
review:
Took a while to get going but eventually got pretty interesting. Malice was the better starting book, for this one the characters mostly stay in the same spot and then some major events happen towards the end so it feels less dynamic than the preceding series.

I will say that this book is darker than Faithful and the fallen which I'm digging. There's some messed up stuff that happens and I hope it gets even darker. I'm also hoping that it's less good vs evil and more gray than FATF, so far it's maybe a little less clear cut, but the bad guys are REALLY bad but the side of good is a little more fuzzy.

Overall an enjoyable read but nothing earth shattering.

title: The Hobbit, or There and Back Again
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
review: Timeless classic. As wondrous as when I first read it as a child. The Andy Serkis narration is sublime.

title: Attack on Titan, Vol. 25
author: Hajime Isayama
review: Feeling morally conflicted and edge of your seat action *chef's kiss*

title: The Heart of What Was Lost
author: Tad Williams
review:
4.5/5

This book is incredibly well done, Tad Williams adds a lot of flavor to his world and poses a lot of moral questions on the nature of what should be done in the aftermath of a war against a seemingly unforgiving enemy. I would agree with criticism of Tad's previous books in the series in that they tend to be longer than they really should be, but here he proves that he can write a great story with a leaner page count and it doesn't lose any of his signature prose or world building.

title: The Simple Path to Wealth: Your Road Map to Financial Independence and a Rich, Free Life
author: J L Collins

title: Rogue Protocol
author: Martha Wells
review:
Pretty lukewarm on this series as a whole, the plot isn't really too compelling so all the enjoyment hinges on the characters. The human characters are fairly bland but some of the robot characters are interesting.

Most likely won't continue this series unless I run out of things to read, there's enough other sci-fi books out there that actually explore interesting ideas that this one won't be a priority to continue.

title: Children of Time
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
I don't want to over praise this book due to recency bias, but it's good. Really good. I think it will be cemented for me as a science fiction classic. Tchaikovsky explores a lot of interesting ideas with nuance and care. Nothing seems ham-fisted and both sides of the conflict or differing philosophies are fairly represented and have you empathizing with both sides which is not easy to pull off.

This also is one of the best if not the absolute best description of aliens I have read. His zoological background makes the encounters and progression of the aliens pretty mind bending and engaging. Feels very realistic and plausible that if the cast of the evolutionary dice were different it could have ended up like this instead.

title: The Black Company
author: Glen Cook
series: The Chronicles of the Black Company, #1

title: Forge of Darkness
author: Steven Erikson
review:
DNF 42%. This is a self-indulgent book weighed down with way too much philosophizing at the expense of characters and plot. Every character will stop on a dime to think about the nature of good and evil, religion, politics; you name it. Even after facing a life or death situation. The main Malazan series at least had a balance but this is off the deep end.

The writing is beautiful, but this is a pain to get through. Was really interested in learning more about the ancient Malazan races but even major plot points here are an enigma and always told in the most impenetrable way possible.

title: Berserk Volume 11
author: Kentaro Miura
review: Really dark, keeps getting better. The emotional weight keeps building up, the action is stellar, and the art is amazing.

title: Shadows Linger
author: Glen Cook
series: The Chronicles of the Black Company, #2

title: The Darkness That Comes Before
author: R. Scott Bakker
review:
Wanted to write down a couple of things just to encourage you to give these books a try. This is a criminally overlooked series and the Goodreads ratings for it are a travesty.

This series is dark, epic, and has great and nuanced characters. Definitely not for the faint of heart or easily offended, but if you are looking for a mature book with amazing writing, deep philosophical questions, and complex political machinations this may be the series for you.

Bakker is a masterclass writer and this series has some of the most compelling mysteries I've ever read, I absolutely devour these books and want to know what happens next so badly. His approach to a book epic in scope is really well done, he eases you into the world piece by piece in this book before the main drive of the series takes place.

title: Galaxy in Flames
author: Ben Counter
review: Definitely a step down from the first two books in the writing and plot. Ends strong but the first half drags pretty hard.

title: Stories of Your Life and Others
author: Ted Chiang
review:
The ideas in this book are incredible. The biggest con is that once you get invested in the story it goes on to the next one, but that's just the effect of the short story format. I'd read a full novel of any of the stories in this book.

The diversity of the stories is a strong point, each one is fairly unique and different than the others and all make you think of different aspects of society, religion, and technology like all good sci-fi should.

title: Dogs of War
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: Rex is a Good Dog

title: Heir of Novron
author: Michael J. Sullivan
review: Nice blend of classic and modern fantasy. Nothing mind blowing, but very entertaining and Sullivan is good at crafting a story that isn't easy to predict and doesn't pull punches when you might expect it to. He also mixes things up a fair bit and you get a lot of variety in the locations and types of stories that he's telling that keep it fresh.

title: Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly
author: Anthony Bourdain
review: No one knows food and the restaurant business like Bourdain. An unflinching look at the debauchery, brotherhood, and grit of working in kitchens. At one point this book is a huge gut punch as Bourdain recounts that he's still alive despite all the drugs, bad decisions that he's made 😢. We miss you Tony.

title: The White Rose
author: Glen Cook
series: The Chronicles of the Black Company, #3

title: The Flight of the Eisenstein
author: James Swallow
review: The best 40k book I've read yet, this one has it all: spaceship battles, creepy mechanized aliens, creepy chaos space creatures, moral dilemmas, politics, great characters and shows important events in a new light.

title: One-Punch Man, Vol. 2: The Secret to Strength
author: ONE

title: The God is Not Willing
author: Steven Erikson
review:
Pretty good, not my favorite Malazan book by far but overall fairly solid. Was definitely missing the epic scale of the other books and even though the book is a lot shorter than the others it does feel like it's treading water a bit waiting for the main events to come about. The writing, especially in the beginning, is excellent. I like Erikson having a more focused story but the actual plot could have had a bit more happen, I'm hoping the next book is a bit faster paced.

One of the biggest negatives for me is there is _a lot_ of marine banter in this one that I enjoyed in the beginning but it just keeps happening and loses its effect after awhile and started to grate on me by the end. Also has some of the weakest characters Erikson has done so far with a couple of notable exceptions. I don't think this one lived up to the amount of hype it had and the payoff wasn't as big as I'd hoped.

title: The Expert System's Brother
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
Tchaikovsky is so creative and each book of his feels distinct and well written in its own way. This one delves into societal aspects and is more of a mix of Fantasy and Sci-fi.

The world also feels real and brutal with some of the best descriptions of various creatures and fauna that are otherworldly and weird but feel realistic. Can't wait to read the next one.

title: The Expert System’s Champion
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: The story went in a direction I wasn't expecting and didn't build off my favorite parts of the first book. Still good writing but didn't quite land completely for me. Reading it back to back it seemed like it didn't quite have continuity with the first one especially in terms of the themes. Almost felt like a different story

title: A Little Hatred
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
This is peak Abercrombie. His writing has improved so much since the initial First Law book. He plays to his strengths here and has a big cast of interesting and funny characters that are morally gray to a tee. Some of the best dialogue in any book.

The plot is also unique and relevant to current day events and has well rounded perspectives on all sides of the issues of industrialization, corruption, power, poor vs rich.

Great first entry that builds off all of the books before so well without rehashing anything that came before. Excited to see where this series goes.

title: Excalibur: A Novel of Arthur
author: Bernard Cornwell
review:
This trilogy is a masterpiece for sure. So good. Feels real and is way darker than I thought it would be.

The interaction between Paganism, Christianity, and the Saxon religion are so compelling and bring a blend of magic that you're never sure if it's superstition or actually having an effect on the plot.

Great characters that you learn to love, hate, and some that are redeemed and some that fall to the temptation of evil.

title: The Trouble with Peace
author: Joe Abercrombie
review:
Too much focus on things I didn't care for and didn't play to Abercrombie's strengths. Definitely enjoyed certain parts but overall much weaker than ALH to me.

Not bad by any means, but I did expect a lot more. Abercrombie is pulling a lot of punches in scenes that could be pivotal and it's losing the impact that they could have had.

title: The Player of Games
author: Iain M. Banks
review:
I'd recommend you to just read Ender's Game instead, it executes an idea like this a lot better.

It's a weird way to tell a story without that much tension or really not explaining the game that well in a book called "Player of Games"

I was tempted to DNF Player of Games, Banks has some of the most bland writing I've ever read. It's neither offensibly bad or good in any way. It's really sort of amazing how the plot is moving forward without much character motivation.

I was thinking it was a 3/5 for awhile but I realized that I wouldn't care if I never found out how it ended. Banks doesn't excel at one thing in particular so the result is that there's many sci-fi authors that you should look to for better humor, world building, ideas.

title: The Judging Eye
author: R. Scott Bakker
review:
Bakker keeps getting better. This is way more of a slow burn, but you spend a lot of time developing and catching up on characters you spent time with in the first trilogy and dealing with the fallout from it.

The world building and lore in this one is next level, also has some deeply disturbing and horrifying scenes; great stuff for grimdark fans.

The writing is some of the best, silky smooth prose and the scenery descriptions really pop and immerse you deeply into the world. Really can't say enough good things, I want to find out what happens really badly.

title: Trollslayer
author: William King
review: Not high-literature by any stretch of the imagination, but a lot of fun. Hits a lot of the notes in Fantasy that I'm looking for, the stories start feeling somewhat similar by the end, but you get a lot of fun monster slaying along the way with the varied factions in the Warhammer world and get to see a couple of iconic locations. Keeble's narration of the audiobook is amazing as well.

title: Exhalation
author: Ted Chiang
review:
Inconsistent. Some stories are great, some are pretty meh. One is so generic I had to DNF it and it was the longest one by a large margin.

This is heavily driven by ideas over characters and the ideas in this one aren't as interesting as Stories of Your Life and Others. The characters are pretty shallow too and hard to connect to.

title: The Wisdom of Crowds
author: Joe Abercrombie
review: Abercrombie grins as he stares at you across the room. The smell is awful. Shit is scattered throughout the room as a giant metal fan sprays it continuously as it pours from buckets above. The only pause is for Abercrombie to fill another bucket, trudge up the stairs and continue the foul smelling onslaught. Needless to say, shit really hits the fan in this book and it just keeps hitting. This is the darkest First Law book yet and is nearly continuous action and has multiple climaxes spaced throughout the novel.

title: The Doors of Eden
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: DNF 33%. I'm normally a big fan of Tchaikovsky but this one is awkward and clumsy. Reads like YA mixed with infodumps. Lots of telling over showing and pop culture references. Don't see any reason to continue unfortunately.

title: A Brightness Long Ago
author: Guy Gavriel Kay
review: Some of the most beautiful writing I've ever read. Great meditation on how our lives often take turns on impulses and decisions early in life. Some of the best writing from the perspectives of people that have just died and the descriptions of death are haunting and moving. Lots to think about on this one.

title: The White-Luck Warrior
author: R. Scott Bakker
review:
This is one of the densest and metaphorical of the series so far which made it a bit of a challenge to read (and required re-reads of many sections), but this series continues to be one of my favorite series. It's getting so dark and bleak, but Bakker's writing remains some of the most beautiful and deep I've read.

This book also has some of the best action in the entire series so far. Each book in the series doesn't end cleanly and makes you want to pick up the next book immediately, so I've found it a challenge to take breaks in-between the books in this second series. This definitely feels like one big story and not individual episodes.

Bakker definitely keeps dangling the promise of answers as a carrot to keep you trudging along the slog of slogs!

title: The Great Ordeal
author: R. Scott Bakker
review: The density and lack of clarity in some big events does put a damper in some of my enjoyment, but still enjoying this series a lot overall. A bit worried we won't get all the answers we're looking for by the end, still a lot of teasing along here even with one book left...so we'll see.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
author: Douglas Adams

title: The Unholy Consult
author: R. Scott Bakker
review:
I finished this a year ago and I'm still thinking about the ending. One of my favorite series of all time.

Please write some more books Bakker 🙏

title: Uzumaki
author: Junji Ito
review: I had to force my way through some of this. The characters and overall plot are pretty weak. The art and some of the ideas are really good, but I need a good story and characters to make me more interested.

title: Skavenslayer
author: William King
review: Skaven, yes yes!

title: Daemonslayer
author: William King
review: These books are incredibly fun and a joy to read. Love all the lore they have and the fast pace of the adventures.

title: A Night in the Lonesome October
author: Roger Zelazny

title: The Willful Princess and the Piebald Prince
author: Robin Hobb

title: Sword Song
author: Bernard Cornwell
review: The best one yet, great battle scenes and character moments. Will miss Keeble's narration greatly, his performance here is amazing

title: Jade City
author: Fonda Lee
review:
Really enjoyed this one overall and it's pretty fast paced and establishes the world and the characters in it well. Good start to the trilogy and excited to pick up the next one.

Writing is pretty straightforward, but describes the action clearly, nothing incredibly deep here but it's quite the page turner and has some good surprises along the way.

title: The Fellowship of the Ring
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
review: Re-reading this has been such a treat, getting so much more out of it this time and have so much more appreciation for it since the first time I read it in middleschool. Even though it's pretty slow, Tolkien is the best worldbuilder that ever lived, there's so much life and lore baked into every page. The Andy Serkis narration is legendary and really brings this to life.

title: Prince of Thorns
author: Mark Lawrence
review: I enjoyed this one a lot more than I expected. The writing is really well put together, was an unexpected strength of the book. The plot goes to some unexpected and unique places, but definitely uses some existing fantasy staples as well. Oh and it is dark and dastardly of course. Jorg is not a good dude. Excited to continue the series.

title: Dragonslayer
author: William King
review: The weakest one yet, but still fun. The romance subplot is not great though

title: Persepolis Rising
author: James S.A. Corey
review: This is one of my favorites in the series so far. Expanse at its best. Really hyped for the last two books. Builds on everything else that has come before really well and sets up the end game. Also has a very good story in itself, so it's not all strictly set-up.

title: Jade Legacy
author: Fonda Lee
review:
There's a lot packed into this book, and the sheer ambition, character work, and plot is enough to make this a five star read. I wouldn't say this is one of my all time favorite reads, or even up there with the best I've read this year, but I did enjoy my time with it. This one reads as a number of story vignettes that utilize the characters we're familiar with through a large chunk of time that has some characters grow old, some grow up, and some die, horribly and tragically.

One of my critiques is that it doesn't feel like a cohesive narrative as much, that while it's very interesting and engaging, what it's building towards thematically doesn't connect with me as much as some of my favorite books. While I admire the ambition here, what the author is trying to comment on and build outside of the plot isn't done as well as some of my other favorite authors might do. That being said, the plot and characters are all really well done and it's fun to read having no idea what can happen next is compelling.

title: The Steel Remains
author: Richard K. Morgan
review:
This one's hard to assign any sort of rating to as it's very out there and weird, but also some of the most graphic content I've ever read. It definitely descends into nihilism at times and almost didn't want to continue the series, but there's enough unique here that I want to give the next one a try at some point.

I didn't think it was as "trope smashing" as others have praised this as being, since there's definitely similar structure to other fantasy books, but maybe the level of depravity counts as smashing tropes? I'm not sure.

title: Brothers of the Wind
author: Tad Williams
series: The Last King of Osten Ard, #0.75
review:
4.5/5 I'm all in on Osten Ard. This is my 7th Osten Ard book I've read this year and the 5th one I've re-read, you could say I'm a fan.

This is an essential novel either before starting Last King of Osten Ard or before Navigator's Children. It's hard to stress just how relevant this book is to that series and I had no idea how much it was until reading Witchwood Crown and Empire of Grass.

These books reward immersion and attention to detail as new mysteries emerge and the lore gets deeper and richer since this is the only prequel novella so far. It's incredibly interesting what the intrinsic mysteries of this world are that even the ancient Zadaya, Hikadaya, and Zinukadaya races disagree and debate on.

The characters Tad creates and has perspectives on here are some of his best where they're easy to empathize with and they're usually trying to do the right thing but go through terrible hardships that they must overcome, great stuff.

Can't praise the series highly enough, some of the most beautiful writing I've ever read and one of the best worlds I've been immersed in in any fantasy series.

title: Empire of Silence
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
**spoiler alert** Re-read in 2023 and it was awesome, especially with having the context of later books.

Review is from original 2021 read:

What an awesome book. Didn't expect it to be as dark as it was, I thought the beginning and ending were very strong, the middle parts weren't as smooth but I liked where it was building towards.

I wasn't expecting the 1984 like surveillance state, thought that was a really cool aspect. I liked how all the influences were worn on its sleeve and definitely got the references to Book of the New Sun (especially the ending where Hadrian says you don't have to read any further, references to torturers, lictors, probably more that I missed).

And the Dune references - fear is a poison, shields and sword combat, thinking machines being illegal, the Chantry being the overarching authority of the universe with atomic weapons.

Didn't think this was overdone and was mixed into a world that made sense and also there was a lot of fucked up social dynamics with class disparity being a huge deal that we see while Hadrian is homeless for a few years and his privilege of being in the upper social class with the contrast of the plague going on only for the plebian class was really interesting and messed up.

I'm definitely interested in what is going on with the Quiet, the part where Hadrian trips balls in the hidden chamber in the ruins was probably my favorite part of the book. The parts with the Cielcin were awesome and learning more about them is really cool and compelling.
