Also the fact that they're not completely buddy buddy with Hadrian makes sense and they actively try to kill him because he promised they'd be released and not killed.

The politics in the book was great, want to learn more about all the houses and figure out more about the religion that considers Earth a God and what actually happened there.

I liked how I didn't really know where the book was going to go and for the most part characters you meet are only there transiently and you don't know who's going to stick around and for how long.

title: The Lesser Devil
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
3.5/5 sort of skippable but there is some interesting stuff in here. Mainly how Crispin and Sabine view Hadrian and their father outside of Hadrian's POV. Some interesting world building, plot was on the weaker side. Some of the world building I sort of had to suspend disbelief that some of the world religions are actually intact in the way we view them today and was hoping for more changes there.

Maybe will appreciate this one more depending on what's in Howling Dark.

title: Cirque Du Freak: A Living Nightmare
author: Darren Shan
review: I'm not sure if I'll rate these, but I have a lot of nostalgia for this series and there's an excellent audio version narrated by Ralph Lister for free on Audible Plus which has been an excellent way to re-read these. The first entry held up really well and I can see why I loved these as a kid. They are surprisingly dark books and very fast paced which makes you want to read them in a single day. Perfect for emerging and existing fans of horror. Very simple and easy to understand writing that doesn't pander down to its intended audience.

title: The Curse of Chalion
author: Lois McMaster Bujold
review:
This is a mixture of literature and fantasy and it's good to know that going in. I have similar feelings for this book as I had for Ursula K Le Guin's The Dispossessed where it's not exactly an easy book to read and you have to take it slow to really absorb what's going on. There's also a fair amount of challenge in navigating how all the characters are addressed, their titles, etc are fairly different and all the relationships between the characters takes a while to get used to. This is a politics heavy book as well, which made some parts drag a bit for me. Most of the time is spent on court politics so if you're not invested in that it can be a bit of a challenge.

The writing is absolutely amazing and one of the best parts of the book. Bujold is a master wordsmith and there's some jaw droppingly gorgeous sections of prose here. Some of the descriptions here are best when you read them slow and deeply imagine the scene and what's going on, it's an immersive read and the world here feels real while also being very strange, and it gets stranger.

The story and plot are slow, really slow. Slower than the Farseer trilogy by far which is part of why this isn't 5 stars for me. Once the plot gets going it's really interesting and there's some unexpected plot elements that are fairly unique and the way magic and the Gods work in this universe is different from how other fantasy books usually work. I'm hoping for successive books that the plot moves a bit quicker and the setting is outside of a royal court which could make for one of my favorite reads if that all lines up with my preferences later on in the series.

title: Howling Dark
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
Re-read 2024:
Just as good or better than I remembered it. Definitely one of my favorite sci-fi books. The experience of exploration and discovery in a richly built universe is incredibly powerful. The re-read was very rewarding and glad I did it before I get the ARC for Disquiet Gods. The foreshadowing is also so clever and hard to notice until you know what you know from later books. Highly highly recommend the series.

Original read 2022:
Please read this series. Weird, epic, philosophical, dark, action packed, introspective, spooky, mysterious, ethereal. This series really comes into its own here and it needs to become way more popular, this entry really blew me away from beginning to end, I enjoyed every minute of this and had no idea where the story would go.

It's always full of surprises and extremely well put together in a way that is internally consistent. I can't wait to read the next one and see where it's going to go. Enjoying the ride.

title: Tunnels of Blood
author: Darren Shan
review: The audiobook for this was absolutely stellar. Ralph Lister's performance is fantastic.

title: Demon in White
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
March 2025 re-read:

Even better on re-read, appreciate the politics way more and so much foreshadowing and lore that's easier to appreciate knowing where things are going. Still like Howling Dark more but this book still slaps.

January 2022 review:

The last book set an incredibly high bar, this one is overall a fantastic entry and Ruocchio packs enough in a single book to warrant trilogies in other series. There's a huge amount of variety and even if certain parts don't click with you it changes things up pretty frequently.

I do prefer Howling Dark to this one, but that's most likely going to be one of if not my favorite book of the year.

Some things that didn't quite land for me were some of the political machinations and times where first person narrative was detrimental to the story being told. Also this does feel like a bit of a middle book where it's connecting the ground shaking changes from Howling Dark and setting up Kingdoms of Death so certain parts can feel reminiscent of what's been done prior in the series.

However, the ambition remains huge here and the scale really gets turned up a notch and there's some crazy stuff that happens that connects to all the books before really well.

The universe that's being built here is so cool and there's a lot that can still be done. I'm anxiously awaiting for the next entry.

title: The Storyteller: Tales of Life and Music
author: Dave Grohl

title: Ogres
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
I received a free copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

This is another excellent Tchaikovsky novella that does a lot in the limited amount of pages. Tchaikovsky is one of my favorite discoveries of the past year and the amount of inventiveness and creativity he has is staggering. Each book I read of his is unique and tackles different ideas.

This book focuses a lot on various classes in this world and the inequality that follows, how the upper class controls the poor through religion, economics, and pure brutalism.

There are a lot of twists and turns along the way, the writing is very tight and effective of conveying the deep ideas that are packed in with a level of nuance and subtlety of his previous works.

Highly recommend, this one is really interesting and very relevant to society today. Another great science fiction book that explores the big ideas and muddy ethics that face us today.

title: Black Stone Heart
author: Michael R. Fletcher
review:
3.5/5

The food and booze descriptions are the standout here, let's be real.

World building and magic system were interesting. Definitely some gray morality in this one but could have used some more subtlety. Book 2 will be make or break for sure, the main plot needed a bit more meat here but for the first 60% I was very invested.

Overall solid in my book but not as dark as I was expecting or hoping. Lots of opportunities to grow into a solid series, maybe tripped up on execution a little bit, but I can see later entries either running with it or fumbling. Interested to read the next book in the next month.

title: Kings of Paradise
author: Richard Nell
review:
Really great character work. The structure of the book is very well done as well, it kind of starts off with only the two main POVs and branches out from there which is a great way to build out the world and plot.

Also you tend to stick with the same character for much longer than other epic fantasy books and you get to see a whole arc from them before it shifts perspective which is a great way to handle a big story.

Overall this book is impressive for a new author and incredibly dark, often bleak, but there's hints of lightness peaking through no matter how narrow the odds of that panning out.

title: Kings of Ash
author: Richard Nell
review:
Amazing, phenomenal, epic, intimate. No middle book syndrome here, actually whatever the opposite of middle book syndrome is what this is. I usually have mixed feelings on "subvert expectations" but this does that in incredibly smart ways that retroactively makes the first book richer. Adds many layers and shades of gray to existing characters and plot points that may have seemed straightforward in the first book but now they're anything but.

I thought the writing was already strong in the first book, but in this one you get really awesome and rousing speeches, great internal monologues, and interesting political machinations. Nell continues to play with the structure of traditional fantasy in interesting ways that makes it exciting to see what's going to happen next, but he does it in a way that is internally consistent and starts panning out to reveal the tapestry of the story that he's revealed slowly and deliberately.

This is very character driven and the characters are one of the huge strengths here, Nell takes a lot of risks with how he divides his time up between his characters, but the result is one of my favorite conflicted characters in all of fantasy that has a lot more layers than initially thought. Maybe one of the downsides is that we get less of some of the other characters, but a lot more focus in the main plot thread also allows for more depth and nuance.

Can't wait to see how it ends.

title: Kings of Heaven
author: Richard Nell
review:
A lot more plot focused than the previous books, the finish line is in sight and most of the book is a mad dash to get there. This book could (should?) have been twice as long and focused on the characters a bit more.

However, there's some really cool moments, world building, and politics here, I've been extremely impressed with how different each book in the trilogy has been. This really nails the landing and is a very satisfying trilogy that doesn't overstay its welcome.

Richard Nell has become an automatic day one buy and read for me, he hits a lot of the notes I'm looking for in dark epic fantasy and his character work is very well done and highly nuanced. I want more! Will be reading the rest of his work soon.

title: Elric of Melniboné
author: Michael Moorcock
review: Pretty basic story, didn't feel like it did anything in particular that well compared to its peers, hasn't aged that well. Would hope that it either stands out with humor, world-building, magic, or action but doesn't really stand out in any of those aspects but is passable in all of these areas. Hoping the next book fleshes out things more, a bit barebones so far.

title: The Fortress of the Pearl
author: Michael Moorcock
review:
A lot more interesting and weird (in a good way) than the first book. Now it's clear that the initial book is just all of Elric's backstory, but it wasn't that unique and fairly formulaic.

This one definitely changes it up, although it seems like a side quest, there are a lot of interesting explorations of the themes in the novel that resonate with me and how to reconcile identity and justice in a culture that may be fundamentally evil. Elric also is exploring more of who he wants to be although he is partially still a slave to Chaos.

Elric is sort of an idiot many times where the only reason he survives is dumb luck or someone swooping in and saving him at the last second as if he's a damsel in distress. That happens a few times here, but Moorcock is growing on me more here and it's becoming more clear what he's trying to say and meditate on here in his series.

I'm more encouraged to continue on now, this series is a weird blend of pulp, dark, and philosophical and with this one it worked for me and I enjoyed it.

title: Allies of the Night
author: Darren Shan
review: Maybe one of the weaker entries, one plot line was pretty dull, but a number of great character moments

title: Hellmouth
author: Giles Kristian
review: Great lil grimdark novella. Kristian describes horrific, dark, and terrifying things in a beautiful way. I need to read more by this author, thought this was fantastic and would have read a full novel based on this story. Reminded me a lot of Between Two Fires, Berserk, and Dark Souls in the best ways.

title: The Sailor on the Seas of Fate
author: Michael Moorcock

title: Sons of Destiny
author: Darren Shan
review: Man, I really liked all of the books before this but the ending was just not good. Going to pretend that it ended a different way

title: Upgrade
author: Blake Crouch
review:
I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

First off, if you're exhausted by COVID or current world events, I'd probably steer clear of this one as it is very clearly inspired by COVID and extrapolates to the near future of the implications of COVID and genetic engineering. The main premise of this is "what if COVID, but it makes you stronger, better, faster, stronger?" Also can be a bit of a downer about the path we're headed down as a species, which is fine, but if you're looking for an escape might not be the best way to do that.

Crouch writes a good thriller and it's easy to read and get through a bunch of chapters in no time, this would make for a good beach read that challenges your thinking a little bit but not too much.

Some of the ideas here are interesting but feel a little rushed and they definitely needed more room to breathe and more page time to get more connected to the characters and dig into the ideas a bit deeper.

It was definitely enjoyable to read, but I'll probably forget about it pretty quickly. It all does feel a bit too familiar of a movie you've seen before but with more of a COVID and current events angle that never feels completely believable in the way that Crichton books can feel.

Would recommend this book to anyone who wants a quick read with a lot of action that does a decent job of creating a near future world and asks some interesting questions about genetic engineering and what it means to be human. Didn't blow me away but I enjoyed my time with it.

title: City of Golden Shadow
author: Tad Williams
review:
This is really like ten books in one, every chapter changes it up and is often in a completely different genre. One of the most ambitious book ones I've read, there's a huge amount of disparate storylines that are distinct and hugely different and it's not clear how they'll all converge, but they're all enjoyable and crafted with care.

Has some pacing issues like pretty much every Tad Williams book I've read which is the biggest issue, but doesn't impact the novel that significantly. The writing is beautiful. Tad Williams is one of my favorite authors for setting a scene and immersing you in a moment, even though the world is strange and often horrifying there's moments of serenity and beauty that take your breath away with how they're described.

title: The Devil All the Time
author: Donald Ray Pollock
review:
Super dark and bleak. There's not really good people in this book, mostly bad people doing bad and trying to get away with it. Also tons of violence, sometimes justified, often not. If there was more internal struggle in the characters would have rated it higher, still really good and entertaining read.

The prose was pretty well done and understated as well. Pollock did a great job at introducing characters and giving them a lot of backstory in a short amount of time. Thematically I think the novel could have done more but there was a fair amount of subtlety to give the senseless violence meaning and you have to look for it to get it; it's not spelled out to you for better or worse.

title: River of Blue Fire
author: Tad Williams
review:
Sort of a love/hate relationship with this one to be totally honest. It's longer than it has any right to be, really and a lot of the plot is wandering around different VR worlds and somehow escaping at the last minute.

However, it's Tad Williams and there's beautiful writing and he's very good at what he does, even though sometimes he needs to move on to the next thing. There's also really cool ideas being explored and still very ambitious. Feels a bit like a middle book because it definitely is, although there's some cool revelations and character moments, but the tension isn't kept up throughout the book, the stakes are high but the characters sort of go on an adventure and usually totally fine by the end of that "episode".

Hoping that the next book is an improvement, I thought the first book was better balanced, still interested to see how things develop in later books. There's really cool and interesting sci-fi concepts being explored and interesting mysteries yet to unfold.

title: Interview with the Vampire
author: Anne Rice
review: The first half was fantastic and one of the best vampire stories I've read. It was an intimate, personal story with interesting philosophical questions and Rice made New Orleans come alive. The second half wasn't as good, sort of takes a weird turn and didn't care for the plot as much. Still very good story, interested to see what happens next at some point in the future.

title: Senlin Ascends
author: Josiah Bancroft
review:
This was a great read, pacing was just right. Got a good balance of world building, character development, and the plot clips away at a steady pace where it's clear that we're making progress towards a larger ending. A weak point was that the action writing wasn't as clear as I would have liked at the end and things got a bit muddled, but prior to that didn't have any issues with the writing and I think in particular the structure of the book is really well done where Bancroft is slowly revealing aspects of the world and characters that make you more invested and not overwhelmed.

Excited to see where the plot goes from here! Really easy to read and I sort of flew through this one unintentionally which is a good sign.

title: Breakfast at Tiffany’s and Three Stories
author: Truman Capote
review: I don't get it. Holly is insufferable. It would be an absolute nightmare to know her in real life.

title: The Black Echo
author: Michael Connelly
review: Bank heists, Vietnam tunnels, crooked cops, the concrete jungle of Los Angeles: all excellent ingredients to a fantastically executed crime story.

title: The Lincoln Lawyer
author: Michael Connelly
series: The Lincoln Lawyer, #1; Harry Bosch Universe, #16
review:
One of my favorite books I've read this year. Liked this more than the first Bosch book that was already fantastic. Mickey Haller is such a great character. "A scumbag defense attorney that's still loved by his two ex-wives and his daughter."

Connelly wrote a hell of a page turner, didn't want to put it down. His pacing is next level good. Thrilling from beginning to end. Only question now is whether to do the next Bosch or Haller book next 🤔

title: Kingdoms of Death
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
June 2025 review:
Yep, still amazing. Agree with everything I wrote in my original review still. If anything this got better with re-read. The beginning of the book hit better this time, I was less in a rush to get to the good bits. I have such a better connection with the side characters on this read knowing where everything is going and their arcs. Just peak sci-fi, very special series. Looking forward to Shadows Upon Time so so much.

March 2022 review:
Even though my expectations were already sky high this book exceeded them. Has amazing lore and world building, great dark moments, and lots of emotional impact. Eagerly awaiting the next book, this is easily one of the best sci-fi series I've read.

Ruocchio's writing has gotten even better, the prose is beautiful even when the subject matter is terrifying and bleak. Can't recommend this series enough, I have my full faith in Ruocchio to deliver a great read.

title: Mountain of Black Glass
author: Tad Williams
review: A step in the right direction, liked this a lot more than the second book. I'm sort of both relieved to finish and interested in what's going to happen next, but will be taking a break before the last book. These books are still too long, but I enjoyed a good majority of this one. Some good plot progression, but there's just a lot of threads going on at once which can get tiring.

title: Arm of the Sphinx
author: Josiah Bancroft
review: Disappointing. I really loved the first book and this was a massive step down. Really did not like the plot and the way the character development and world building was done in this one. Overall felt clumsy and uninteresting to me. I might still try the third book, but the overall tone and themes in this book are a big miss for me.

title: The Shadow of What Was Lost
author: James Islington
review:
Read about 60% of this, don't want to finish. This series isn't for me. It's decent but nothing about it is that interesting to me and for the most part aside from some twists is fairly standard fantasy genre fare. Reminds me the most of Stormlight Archive and the Lord of the Rings. Has a lot of the things that make Sanderson not click with me.

If I had read this as one of my first fantasy series would probably have been more interested. The writing overall is fairly amateur, the dialog is pretty awkward, and the characters are thin. I'm not as driven by the plot of books so much as the quality of the writing, characters, and the world so this one doesn't have what I'm looking for.

title: Berserk Volume 26
author: Kentaro Miura
review: Badass

title: The Grace of Kings
author: Ken Liu
review:
I absolutely loved every minute of this book. Ken Liu has the potential to be one of my favorite writers. I have major respect for authors with a strong vision of what they want their story and narrative to be even if it's a little outside of normal conventions and sticking with it without any compromises.

This is definitely a dense and challenging read and demands that you pay attention to get the full experience, often Liu will not re-introduce characters even though there are a lot of them, and you often get a short flashback that fleshes out their backstory after being introduced to them. I'm in love with his writing style and he gets me to care about new characters faster than pretty much any author I've read before.

Liu's prose is top notch, I'm a self-admitted prose snob and there's no faster way to get me to quit a book than poor writing. Grace of Kings has gorgeous sections that relate humanity to nature, have deep introspective looks into family, nobility, philosophy and they're all interweaved flawlessly.

I'm also a theme-driven reader and the themes Liu explores in this book are tremendous, there's a ton of subtext in the book which rewards an attentive read. I was thinking of listening to this on audio but I'd highly recommend against that, there's a lot of section breaks and pauses that only really come across well in the physical text.

This felt like a whole trilogy or series in a single book, a lot happens and the third person omniscient perspective really helps move things along, I can see this being contentious, but I personally love the risk Liu takes with this perspective since it's not common. It allows Liu to jump around and give the important events in the plot without restrictions.

Highly recommend this book, it's among the best I've read. Can't wait to continue the series, it's been the most excited I've been about an author's work in quite some time.

title: The Wall of Storms
author: Ken Liu
review:
For people who struggled with the first book I think this one might be more in the wheelhouse of a traditional fantasy narrative and be more appealing to people who had issues with the Grace of Kings. It's less of a fable and legend like the first book and more of a modern plot structure. Also the female characters are way better in this one and often overshadow the male characters in most ways.

I really loved every moment of this one again, even though it's almost a thousand pages I didn't want it to end. I do think I personally liked the structure and themes of the first book more but this one had a superior plot and really interesting politics.

Excited to continue the series and see how it all ends. Liu is really good at giving a full cohesive narrative per book so it doesn't leave you hanging and a lot of the threads are wrapped up with enough to make you interested in the next books.

The battles in this book are some of the best I've read, I really didn't expect that from the series but it's been a nice surprise. The technology and war dynamics are always getting changed up which keeps things fresh from battle to battle and book to book.

The prose is also gorgeous as in the first book, but it felt like Liu pulled back in a lot of ways from the first book and delves less into descriptions and poetic nature metaphors. Maybe some people thought it was self indulgent, but I never did and I loved it. I really liked those sections in the first book, but they're less present here and the plot takes more of a center stage for better or worse.

title: She Dreams in Blood
author: Michael R. Fletcher
review:
There's definitely cool moments and interesting ideas in this book, more so than the first book. In isolation I like this one more than the first one. However overall as a series I'm souring on it.

The main character and first person POV is frustrating to read about. His internal struggle is just not compelling and his romance interests are fairly juvenile. The character development was poorly done, the plot didn't move far enough in this one. It's more about the spectacle here and the themes and overarching narrative are falling flat.

title: World Without End
author: Ken Follett
review:
An epic tome of historical fiction. Pillars of the Earth made a big impression on me and I liked this even more. It took a while to get going but Follett does an incredible job developing rich characters and torturing them in dastardly ways. He writes one of the most evil characters I've ever read here and does it in a way that you love to hate.

Highly recommend this series and will be reading a lot of Follett in the future. The audiobooks narrated by John Lee are oddly soothing and easy to get through despite the book being absolutely massive. Pillars was a quicker read but this one was more complex and varied. I had a lot of connections with the characters and some of the plot lines were very compelling.

title: The Curse of the Mistwraith
author: Janny Wurts
review:
Very enjoyable first book, I definitely read this faster than I normally do which is a good sign. This book is closer to classical fantasy than modern fantasy but there's hints that things might get more complex as the series goes on.

I don't think this would really work as a standalone even though on Goodreads it says that this is the first arc. There's so many unresolved questions that it'd be pretty unsatisfying to stop here. The book ends at a logical point, but it's clear that there's a lot that needs to happen for things to be wrapped up.

The writing style is complex and dense but also usually stems from the word choice and sentence structure than the actual plot. Sometimes the narrative and dialog blend together with the third person omniscient perspective, so it's not the best execution of this style. However the prose is gorgeous. Some of the best landscape and scenery descriptions I've read as well as some fantastic dialog. This is probably the main draw for me and is very immersive.

The magic is awesome in this book. Very high magic series with big impact in the plot and the world. The action is also really well done which was a bit of a surprise to me, but the battles and even smaller scale events have a lot of tense moments.

title: The Brass Verdict
author: Michael Connelly
series: The Lincoln Lawyer, #2; Harry Bosch Universe, #19

title: Odin's Wolves
author: Giles Kristian
review: Some great fart jokes

title: All the Seas of the World
author: Guy Gavriel Kay
review:
I would not recommend reading this before reading Lions, Sarantine Mosaic, Children of Earth and Sky, and A Brightness Long Ago. There's a lot of references and building off those books. I read all of these and was still lost at times. I also probably missed a lot doing audio on this one, there's the most POV shifts and nuance in the narrative than all the books of his I've read so far.

Probably the most dense and complex GGK book yet for better or worse. The writing is still beautiful, the plot is a bit overly complicated, and the character moments are pretty good. Not my favorite GGK, but still pretty good. Was hoping for something as good as A Brightness Long Ago, but that's my favorite of his so it's a high bar.

title: The Only Good Indians
author: Stephen Graham Jones
review: Man this is really bad. Not convinced this wasn't ghostwritten by three sixth graders in a trench coat.

title: The Gunslinger
author: Stephen King
review: Really good the second time around, caught a lot more of the references and knowing where the story is going makes it make a lot more sense.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
review: Masterpiece. A classic in every sense of the word. So many layers and also very engaging to read. Just absolutely outstanding and hard to put down.

title: The Veiled Throne
author: Ken Liu
review:
The first 60% is some of the best in the whole series.

The last 40% was more uneven with one storyline taking a lot of page time. I might have snipped out part of this and made it a novella because it was just very different and a big page count, but it does matter for the narrative, just the level of detail was very different from the rest of the series.

The ending was really good despite this being a split book. Really good set up for the final book.

Overall very good for me despite one storyline that wasn't my favorite but I think compared to everything else I've read this book is in the upper tier and I'm looking forward to Speaking Bones.

This has some amazing villains that I love to hate and so many of the characters get great development in this entry. Liu made me feel a lot of things, his thematic writing is some of the best I've read and the way he develops technology and integrates it in the story is mind blowing and unique.

Ken Liu is a massive talent and this is becoming one of my favorite series.

title: A Man at Arms
author: Steven Pressfield
review:
The Road with the Roman Terminator across ancient Israel.

Pretty different from Pressfield's other works, always feel entertained and learn something at the same time. More of an intimate story with fewer characters and interesting stakes. Great meditations on the intersection of religion and history.

title: Equal Rites
author: Terry Pratchett
review:
Even though I've heard that this is one of the weaker Discworld books I really liked it. The plot is one of the weaker aspects but the imagination, wit, and humor of Pratchett is on full display.

I listened to the new audiobooks recently made and the production quality is great as well as the narration, where otherwise it's harder to work these in between my more "serious" reads. Planning to continue with the Witches Discworld books here soon.

title: The Drawing of the Three
author: Stephen King
review: Second time I've read this and enjoyed it a lot more this time. This book is nuts and never read anything like it before or since. Lots of good fish out of water moments and humor. King is the master of character development and these moments are even better on a re-read.

title: The Court of Broken Knives
author: Anna Smith Spark
review:
I liked this overall but there's a few fairly significant issues with the series. The writing style is very good and she mixes the grotesque and the beautiful very well, it's clear that Spark has a deep understanding of what grimdark is.

My big issues are with the instalove in the plot, the character work with the two main characters, and the world building. The secondary characters are all pretty well done but the world never quite makes complete sense and the two main characters I don't have much connection with and it's difficult to say what is actually motivating them.

Overall this book is just ok for me and definitely in a tier below Bakker or Ash and Sand (grimdark I consider to be the pinnacle of the genre).

title: The Waste Lands
author: Stephen King
review: Probably the most cliffhanger ending I've ever read but the rest is fantastic.

title: The Ships of Merior
author: Janny Wurts
review:
I'm really disappointed in this one. I really liked the first book and I felt like this was completely bungled in execution.

The sentence to sentence structure is well done but the overarching plot and characters did not move forward enough. Really slow and I had to force myself through parts of this.

I'm not feeling that connected to the characters and the main driver for me in this series is the magic and the mysteries going on in the background. Those elements were very minor in this entry. Also there were a few moments that were supposed to have more impact where I just didn't feel anything.

I'll give the third book a try but I really did not click with how this story was told.

title: Swan Song
author: Robert McCammon
review: Masterpiece. Loved every page of this. Easily one of the best books I've read. Will be reading a lot of McCammon soon.

title: Saga, Volume 1
author: Brian K. Vaughan
review: The pacing is really good, interested to see where this goes. Some interesting characters and pretty brutal things happening already.

title: Bear Head
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
This is one of Tchaikovsky's best. Very different from Dogs of War but builds off and expands on the themes of the previous books. Really awesome blend of great characters and cool ideas which is what made Dogs of War one of my all time favorite sci-fi books.

The political and social commentary isn't subtle here but I liked it even though it's clear what current political atmosphere he is commenting on, but I could see that bothering some people. It's easy to get inspiration from the real world for villains in a fictional book unfortunately for us.

Tchaikovsky is a massive talent and the extent of his imagination and creativity is mind blowing. Love his work.

title: Genghis: Birth of an Empire
author: Conn Iggulden
review: I liked this and think it's competently written but didn't have much of an emotional connection with the characters or plot. May continue with the next book but this didn't quite mesh with my expectations. I've liked other historical fiction that I have read previously more.

title: Saga, Volume 6
author: Brian K. Vaughan
review: This series is amazing, can't stop reading it.

title: The Tower of Living and Dying
author: Anna Smith Spark
review: This redeemed the series for me and I'm excited to read the last book. Retroactively made the first book better. Interesting plot developments, great action, and beautiful prose. I do think that the world building overall isn't the best and wouldn't put this in the top tier of fantasy series but this is a fun grimdark series and Spark is an author to watch for.

title: Saga, Volume 9
author: Brian K. Vaughan
review: 💔😭. So good but I am not ok

title: Saga, Volume 10
author: Brian K. Vaughan
review: I would like more please, k thx.

title: Lancelot
author: Giles Kristian
review:
A character focused slow burn that packs in a lot of emotions. Really should be read after the Warlord Chronicles by Cornwell because while I loved this, those are much better and these books are inspired by them and offer an interesting contrast to the plot of the Warlord Chronicles. I just would wait awhile after reading those before this because there are definitely similar aspects.

Has some absolutely gorgeous writing and is a very good coming of age story with some action interspersed.

title: Candide
author: Voltaire
review: Candide had a real rough life, take that optimists 😂

title: Queen Amid Ashes
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
The side stuff in Sun Eater continues to just be ok for me even though I absolutely love the main series. Very solid story but it doesn't have the aspects that make me love the main series. Well written but the plot I thought was just ok.

Also felt a bit weird after reading Kingdoms of Death. Would recommend reading this after Howling Dark instead because the series changes so much after that.

title: Speaks the Nightbird
author: Robert McCammon
review:
A colonial mystery horror whodunnit witch trial with Sherlock Holmes vibes, what's not to like?

McCammon has written another masterpiece here, the atmosphere and environment that he builds here is nothing short of extraordinary, it really feels like you're in the age of the frontier colonial America; superstition is high and knowledge / trust in science is low and the horror of the ignorance of humanity is in full force as they see the Devil in every shadow and misread signs from God in day to day life.

The character work here is exceptional as well, Corbett is a great character and you get a lot of backstory from him, his mentor, and other characters as well in a way that's natural during the narrative.

The themes McCammon explores are very interesting and poignant, he uses his prose to delve beneath the surface of a great plot to elevate the narrative and ask the big questions of good vs evil and the folly of man. It's interesting what has changed and also frightening what has stayed the same, the horror found in the souls of our fellow humans can be scarier than the demons in the darkest of corners of the colonial swamps.

I pretty much devoured this and the mysteries are very interesting and come together in a perfect way that is nothing short of genius, the way McCammon plots out his books works so well for me.

Had to restrain myself from starting book 2 immediately. I can't wait to see what Mr Corbett will be up to next.

title: Speaking Bones
author: Ken Liu
review:
Every book has been a 5/5 and it's easily one of my all time favorite series. I'm sad that it's over but thought the ending was fantastic and tied everything together from the series so well. Ken Liu is definitely an autobuy and read day one author for me now, his writing clicks with me so well. So glad I picked up this series.

At a certain point I stopped having any sort of criticism of the series and was just soaking it in and enjoying it, such a huge ambitious series that is unlike anything else I have read. I'm really in awe of what Liu has accomplished here, absolutely masterful stuff and he wrapped things up in such a satisfying and cohesive way with so much to think about going forward.

This is the perfect blend of philosophy, theme, characters, action, horror, technology this series really has it all and there's so much depth and meat to the series. Such an accomplishment that breaks out of any genre definition, my hats off to Mr Liu, will be reading everything that he's written or will write going forward.

title: Vampireslayer
author: William King
review: This was an incredibly fun listen. Probably the least action in the whole series but that was a good thing. Interesting vampire and tomb king lore. A good change of pace after the other books and the huge climax in the last book.

title: Warhost of Vastmark
author: Janny Wurts
review:
Going to pause the series, probably won't continue. The writing is very good but the plot progression is incredibly slow. I am interested in Wurts' other books though at some point.

I didn't feel much connection with the characters. The overall plot is interesting but the majority of the page count does not focus on the plot points I am most interested in and the books have already tread similar ground for each book in the series so far.

Really wanted to like this but it didn't click for me enough to continue this huge series.

title: Fire & Blood
author: George R.R. Martin
review: I don't think GRRM could have written this any better, it's great. The best history of the Targaryens that I could imagine. Really interesting, dark, and has a surprising amount of character moments even when told through the history retelling format.

title: We
author: Yevgeny Zamyatin
review: This was fine, but every other dystopian book I've read has been much better.

title: The Queen of Bedlam
author: Robert McCammon
review:
This series is amazing. McCammon does plotting and characters incredibly well. I'm pumped for the next book. I hope the whole series is just as good.

Less horror aspects than the first book but still some creepy moments, the mystery and the plot and the way it comes together is masterful.

title: Howls from the Dark Ages: An Anthology of Medieval Horror
author: P.L. McMillan
review: There's some really good stuff in this short story collection. Really true to form medieval horror that exemplifies the genre. Evil priests, nuns, creepy castles and knights, horrible plagues, spooky forests; a lot of variety and some great themes as well, only a couple of stories that were just ok. Most were excellent and would like to read more from a few of these authors.

title: Giantslayer
author: William King
review: I'll never get tired of Gotrek saying how much he hates elves haha. We get a great elf character to accompany our heroes in this one, the dynamics of the group were very well done and fun. I loved all these Gotrek and Felix books by William King, hoping Nathan Long's hold up as well.

title: The House of Sacrifice
author: Anna Smith Spark
review:
This totally shit the bed. I really liked the second book and this drops the ball completely, unfortunately. I'm unclear why this series was written and didn't seem to be planned out well and it just sort of ends without any satisfying conclusions or character development. No thematic climax and some really odd choices about where the plot goes and the world building ends up being thin.

The writing style was overdone and actively worked against telling a good story, whereas the other books were much better.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
review:
The philosophy, themes, and prose are quite good in this novel. The plot could have enhanced these aspects a bit more, the first half I thought had a compelling story and then there were a few strange asides that didn't build on what came before and it didn't quite ramp up in ways that would have been more satisfying and reinforced the themes a bit better.

The characters and dialogue were also pretty well done, the characters especially all are flawed and have strong philosophical views of the world that are often opposing and have a satirical Socratic dialog flair for viewpoints that at first can appear absurd and then become more logical which in turn causes the reader to question their own viewpoints.

I'll probably be thinking about this book for a while, I think it could have been a bit stronger with some changes to the execution and how the story developed, but it's definitely worth a read.

title: Camelot
author: Giles Kristian
review: I might like this even more than the first book, but I'll have to think about it. The writing is incredible as are the themes tackled. The prose is interwoven so well into the plot as are the themes of being in the shadow of your father and the sins committed before you were born. Also the surviving characters have a huge amount of trauma and things to wrap their minds around after the events of the first book. Hope there's another entry in this series in the future, I really enjoyed this and looked forward to listening to it every day.

title: The Importance of Being Earnest
author: Oscar Wilde
review: One of the wittiest things I've read, pretty hilarious.

title: Eversion
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
4.5/5

I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Highly recommend it for anyone looking for a sci-fi book that has some really intriguing mysteries. This was my first Reynolds and it won't be my last.

The less you know about this book going in the better. Going in blind is very satisfying, just make sure you have some patience with it as it won't be quite what you expect in the beginning, but things are slowly revealed and it's pretty mind blowing.

This kind of sci-fi is usually criticized for having weak characters but I connected with a number of them here and they're all fairly distinct and have interesting backgrounds. I was definitely invested in them and how they would fare in the challenges that come up throughout the story.

title: Boy's Life
author: Robert McCammon
review:
Man this got me good. Nostalgia distilled to a bitter sweet brew. Perfectly captures the magic of youth and harkens back to a simpler time. One of the best books I've read. You think I'd be tired of saying that after finishing another McCammon book. It's almost annoying how good he is at writing.

Every chapter is something new and interesting much like Swan Song and he incorporates a complex and intriguing mystery much like his Matthew Corbett series.

A masterpiece.

title: The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet
author: Becky Chambers
review:
Basically the book version of chilling with your crew in Mass Effect and helping them solve their problems.

Some really good characters, the stakes aren't too low either because the personal issues can be high consequence for the characters involved, which is good. Maybe needed a bit more of an overarching plot but was still interesting.

Also the galaxy isn't all happy go lucky, there's wars going on and some of the characters have trauma from wars on their home planets, genocide, etc, which I think this series can have a reputation where it's in an unrealistic reality, which isn't quite true.

The crew is all really nice to each other which is refreshing and wholesome, some really good found family dynamics.

The highlight of the book is learning about all the strange alien cultures and doing the side quests where you meet some of the crew's family on their alien planets.

Will be continuing the series, I liked this more than I expected.

title: The Return of the King
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
review: It doesn't get any better than this. Loved this even more than the first time I read this many years ago. I appreciate it much more this time for what it has done for the genre which is still an amazing story on its own.

title: Ashes of Man
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
July 2025 review:
I appreciate what Ruocchio is doing here a lot more this time and reading this right after Kingdoms of Death helps a lot, as the beginning of the book is very much the falling action of KoD. Also I now know what happens in Disquiet Gods and this book makes it possible for that one to be my favorite in the series so far. Still peak sci-fi but definitely a different flavor to the rest of the series in this entry. So many hard hitting moments and even better on re-read, getting way more attached to the side characters this time around.

August 2022 review:
I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

This is going to be as vague as possible and not have any spoilers.

This might be my least favorite Sun Eater book by a comfortable margin. However, since the bar is so high it's still an excellent entry and sets up the next (final?) book to be my favorite in the whole series.

There were a lot of things hinted at in this book that weren't involved in the plot but the ending definitely has a lot of interesting things set up for it.

Since this was originally supposed to be the second half of Kingdoms of Death, I did prefer what happened in Kingdoms of Death by a fairly large margin because of the aspects of the series it dealt with and this book mainly deals with the fallout of Kingdoms of Death and set up for the last book.

Although it definitely has some major events occur, I found myself hoping that the things this book hinted at would be tackled instead of what we got. That's not to say that the plot here isn't interesting but I'm highly anticipating the next entry because it's easy to imagine it being even better.

Overall this is one of my favorite sci-fi series ever and I can't wait to see how it ends. Ruocchio continues to be a massive talent and is full of surprises.

title: The Three-Body Problem
author: Cixin Liu
review:
Even though this has some rough edges, this is one of the best sci-fi books I've read and the ideas explored here are mind blowing.

This is probably the "hardest" sci-fi book I've read where Liu goes deep into the physics and some of the technical details about why the things explored here might be possible. I personally loved this aspect of the book but I could see it causing issues for others.

At times it feels like reading physics proofs and theorems, but in a dramatized way, he also takes interesting applications of computer science concepts that were pretty unexpected to me and that I appreciated a lot.

This book gets criticized for the thin characters which I think overall is fair; it definitely focuses on the ideas and sci-fi concepts, but I didn't think that the characters were poorly written, a couple are interesting and even funny. He definitely sort of puts this on the side about halfway through the book and focuses primarily on the ideas, which I'm ok with.

Really looking forward to the next two books as I've heard they're even better. I'm really glad to have read this and kind of mad at myself for waiting so long. Definitely a unique style of sci-fi that is sort of a more technical version of Clarke in a lot of ways. Can't say I've read anything quite like this even though it uses familiar sci-fi concepts, the way they are blended together and executed is really interesting.

title: Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell
author: Susanna Clarke
review: This was good, but it's just too damn long and not really building towards anything.

title: The Providence Rider
author: Robert McCammon
review:
It's safe to say that this series is definitely one of my all time favorites now. McCammon really utilizes and pays off a lot of stuff he's been setting up in the past few books here. Just a masterful plot that has a lot of interesting threads that all tie together in a satisfying way. Highly recommend this series and this book is in the tier of the first two books which are some of McCammon's best.

Really excited to continue this series, it's a ton of fun, has excellent writing, and interesting themes and characters that feel alive.

title: The Gap Into Conflict: The Real Story
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
review: The main character is one of the worst people you'll ever meet and the book is pretty damn bleak. Has a very pulpy feel and is absolutely grimdark. The story in this one is pretty basic and it's hard to tell what the overall series will be about. Some interesting world building and cool space battles. I'm interested enough to continue with the next one.

title: The Dark Forest
author: Cixin Liu
review: This book has definitely objectively weak points and some pretty bad character development... However I just love the ideas explored and some of the aspects I'll be thinking about for quite some time to come. Very different from the first book in many ways so the style can be a bit jarring, once I got into it though I really enjoyed it.

title: Wolves of the Calla
author: Stephen King
review: I love the number 19

title: The Gap Into Vision: Forbidden Knowledge
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
review:
So this is the most nihilistic and bleak series I've read so far, yep it's pretty rough to read at times. Donaldson roughly prioritizes

1. Torturing and abusing his characters
2. Interpersonal politics
3. Cool sci-fi stuff

in that order. The first half of the book is definitely some of the most hopeless and brutal stuff I've read, the second half prioritizes cool sci-fi stuff a lot more thankfully and has a lot of interesting setup for the rest of the series.

title: The Silver Spike
author: Glen Cook
series: The Chronicles of the Black Company, #3.5
review: Going to shelve this for now, Black Company isn't for me. Hard for me to care about it.

title: Song of Susannah
author: Stephen King
review: Liked this maybe a little bit less than the other books but still really enjoyed it. Also the thing that bothers other people about this book I really enjoyed and it seemed to fit thematically with the rest of the series. Nervous about the last book because I know it doesn't land with a lot of people, but so far I'm a big fan of the series.

title: Academic Exercises
author: K.J. Parker
review:
Really enjoyed this short story collection. He writes a great rougish smart asshole type character from first person really well and it doesn't get old even though his characters have similar personalities. He also understands military history very well and the fighting feels authentic.

His characters usually have unique careers that are outside what you're used to in other fantasy stories such as engineers, alchemists, scholars, and academics. Even his wizards are misunderstood philosophers and scientists.

Looking forward to reading more by him in the future.

title: The Dark Tower
author: Stephen King
review:
3.5/5

I liked this one, didn't love it. It had a lot of strange decisions and wasted potential, King sort of just writes what he feels like writing at times and doesn't plan things out in a way that would be overall more satisfying. Some of the ideas are interesting but I felt like he needed to tie things up a bit more with previous books and the endings for many of the characters weren't satisfying, particularly for many of the antagonists.

Overall probably my least favorite Dark Tower book. I did really enjoy the series overall and it's a very unique and interesting series that is weird and out there in many ways which makes it impossible to tell what direction it'll go into next.

title: The Paper Menagerie and Other Stories
author: Ken Liu

title: A Column of Fire
author: Ken Follett
review:
4.5/5

I liked this the least out of the other Kingsbridge books but it's still better than most other books I've read. I've become addicted to Follet's style of intricate plots powered by realistic characters that are important to historical events.

This one has a bit of a larger scale which caused the characters to be a bit less sharp and have moments that didn't hit as hard as some in the previous books. The conflict between the Protestants and Catholics in this book is really interesting and makes this one more about espionage and politics than the conflicts in the town of Kingsbridge itself. Follet's exploration of religion as a human organization is very interesting and I think he handles perspectives on both sides fairly.

I'll definitely be reading more Follett in the near future and I hope to enjoy his work as much as I have this series, really top tier historical fiction that is very compelling and page turning despite their hefty size. Highly recommend.

title: Freedom of the Mask
author: Robert McCammon
review: Very good book that goes in interesting directions but also treads some similar ground to one of the previous books. Ends on a bit of a cliffhanger which is now two of these books in a row to do so, but sets up the next book well. Overall still enjoying this series a lot and the writing can be quite beautiful at times with great characters.

title: Death's End
author: Cixin Liu
review:
I made this review very non-spoiler for those interested in the series as a whole.

This is definitely one of my favorite sci-fi books and series, Liu has a huge amount of really cool and often crazy ideas packed into this one. He could have gone the easy path for this final book but he went down the more interesting path and the story goes in directions you wouldn't expect after the end of book 2. This book is incredibly heavy and dark at times, I loved it but it took some time to chew on the ideas and the implications of the plot developments. There's a healthy dose of nihilism in this book, but often sci-fi is a bit too optimistic for my tastes and this has a good kick in the teeth for overly optimistic sci-fi. You could probably label parts as grimdark sci-fi as there's some definite bleak moments that are intense and graphic as well as existentially disturbing.

I'll be thinking about this series for quite some time, I absolutely loved my time with it and this is the reason I read sci-fi in general. I can see why this wouldn't be for everyone but personally this is right up my alley. Will be interested in anything Liu comes out with in the future.

title: Sixteen Ways to Defend a Walled City
author: K.J. Parker
review: KJP sort of writes the same protagonist every time, but the smart rougish engineer character Orhan does click with me and the narrative voice is light and amusing. KJP also has a great understanding of medieval warfare and siege weapons so the war and engagements all feel realistic and are often about things going sideways and how to overcome it. Overall a very enjoyable listen and I really enjoy his style of writing.

title: Misery
author: Stephen King
review:
Absolutely loved it, definitely one of my favorite King books now. I really enjoy the lack of supernatural elements as well.

What King can do with two characters in a single location is mind blowing, it stays interesting, exciting, and horrific until the end. Annie Wilkes is a great character and antagonist. Lots of disturbing stuff here to chew on.

The commentary and themes of an author's relationship with his fans, his work, and himself lands really well and you can tell it is almost autobiographical as some of the best stories are. A really unique horror story that I'll be thinking about for a long time, should have read this sooner.

title: Priest of Bones
author: Peter McLean
review:
*Dies in mid*

One of the most aggressively average books I've read in quite some time. It was competently written but I didn't feel much reading it. I won't be continuing.

title: Cloud Cuckoo Land
author: Anthony Doerr
review:
I really liked this one and was engaged from beginning to end. I do think having this many storylines made each storyline progress a lot slower than I would have liked and I didn't connect with some of the characters as much as I hoped, but I still think it's mostly successful in hitting the feels.

I also was a bit unsatisfied with the ending and was hoping things would tie together a bit more, they did in some aspects but for the amount of balls in the air across space and time was hoping for a larger payoff. Reminds me of Fredrik Backman but with less quirky characters (which can be a good thing if you're not in the mood for that). Will like to read Doerr's other book at some point in the future, he definitely intrigued me and glad I read this, but think he could write a different book that lands even better for me.

title: City of Last Chances
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
3.5/5

I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Tchaikovsky is one of my favorite science fiction writers and with his fantasy I don't have a great record with as I've DNFed Doors of Eden and had issues with Guns of the Dawn.

This book throws you in the deep end to start as there's a lot going on in the city of Ilmar with a lot of different POVs most of which are in different factions and parts of the city. The number of different characters is a strength and a weakness of the book where there's a lot of interesting things to keep track of and I really enjoyed the beginning to the middle of the book.

One thing that surprised me was the amount of horror elements. I really liked this aspect of the book and think Tchaikovsky does this well where it's unexpected and adds some cool elements of chaos to the book.

The ending is a bit weaker though for me as I didn't feel completely satisfied with how everything tied together and some of the mysteries that were set up in the beginning didn't pay off as much as I hoped.

The characters are all interesting and well done, they're sufficiently gray as are the rebel factions where it's a bit more complicated than rebels good, occupiers bad.

Overall I think this was a bit too ambitious for a standalone and needed more time to incorporate the different elements of the book either by being much longer or a part of a series. Also cutting some aspects could have made what's there a bit stronger.

I'm glad I read this book and there's a lot of good stuff in it, it's just a bit hard to review and think with a few changes it could have been much stronger.

title: The Gap Into Power: A Dark and Hungry God Arises
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
review:
Easily the best in the series. Donaldson handles expanding the scope really well. This has to be one of the most complex political books I've read. Most of the characters have hidden agendas and their allegiances change depending on the advantages it brings them, makes for an exciting and dynamic read.

The climax of the book is awesome and the way everything ties together is exciting and has cool implications for the next books.

title: The Lesser Dead
author: Christopher Buehlman
review: This is a really fun first person vampire story set in New York City in the 1970s. Lots of brutality and visceral moments from our wise cracking narrator. Some really creepy moments as well, easy to read and I enjoyed this quite a bit. Buehlman's writing is great here, he knows what makes horror work.

title: The Exorcist
author: William Peter Blatty
review: I like the movie substantially more and it works better in a visual medium. The pacing was a bit wonky, some sections of dialog go on for too long. There's a lot of creepy stuff that was good so enjoyed some parts well enough.

title: Pandora's Star
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review:
Biiiigggg sci-fi book. Actually amazed at how much I devoured this considering the size. It's not as dense as I thought and the prose is nice and readable with a good amount of descriptions of the world and landscapes. The characters are also very good and I ended up caring about a lot of them.

This isn't actually as idea heavy as some other sci-fi books, the focus is more about the plot, the world building, and the characters, although there are cool ideas a lot of them stem from the technology developed and how that affects society at large.

Really happy I read this and starting the next big boi immediately.

title: Judas Unchained
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review:
Wrapped up in a really satisfying way and a big climax to the end. The action is awesome and the plot and amount of POVs is really complex. Definitely a top tier space opera. The ideas aren't as focused on as other sci-fi novels which is good to know if you're looking for a particular style.

Will definitely be following up with the Void trilogy in a few months and interested to see where the Commonwealth is headed. Hamilton is definitely on my radar in a big way now.

title: How to Rule an Empire and Get Away with It
author: K.J. Parker
review:
The premise for the book is really good and different from the first book but it sort of loses steam about halfway through and the protagonist isn't as involved in the plot as he really should be.

Probably my least favorite KJP story so far but there are moments that I liked and enjoyed the writing a bit, just didn't feel like it cohesively tied together that well. I'll read the last book and see what happens.

title: Why We Sleep: Unlocking the Power of Sleep and Dreams
author: Matthew Walker
review:
This is a horror book. Horrifying if you're not completely satisfied with your sleep life. Basically lack of sleep is affecting most of the industrialized world and killing us and making us unhappy and unhealthy in a myriad of ways and this is scientifically proven.

There's not a lot of answers for how to fix this unfortunately but there's some suggestions that might be helpful. The world does need to change its relationship with sleep and this helps shed some light on the reality of how humans sleep and why they need to do so.

A lot of the studies in the book are incredibly interesting and some are mind blowing with some of the implications including the ability to influence dreams and early ways to read brain waves and actually figure out what someone is dreaming about.

Highly recommend this book, such an interesting read, but still figuring out how to apply the learnings to my own life.

title: Shaman's Crossing
author: Robin Hobb
review:
I really liked the beginning and end of this book but the middle was a bit of a drag for me. I'll be reading the next book, there's enough plot hooks to make me think that I will like Forest Mage more than Shaman's Crossing.

The writing was pretty good, but definitely not at the levels of Return of the Elderlings which is my favorite fantasy series. This series is a lot more plot focused than ROTE and you don't get as much development into character relationships as that series which is where Hobb's strengths lie. I definitely didn't dislike this, but it did feel like a fairly standard story with some hints at deeper themes under the surface, they just don't appear that much here.

title: Pushing Ice
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
I really enjoyed this a lot. Reynolds grabs you right away with a couple interesting mysteries that have big implications for their scientific impact.

This book also was much different from what I was expecting, I was expecting something a bit more grounded and having harder scientific foundations, but I did really like what I ended up getting.

Will be reading more Reynolds very soon, both of the standalone novels I've read have been hits with me.

title: Blade of the Immortal, Volume 1: Blood of a Thousand
author: Hiroaki Samura

title: Blade of the Immortal, Volume 2: Cry of the Worm
author: Hiroaki Samura
review: Way better than the first volume

title: Blade of the Immortal, Volume 3: Dreamsong
author: Hiroaki Samura

title: The Gap Into Madness: Chaos and Order
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
review:
4.5/5

In hindsight this is my favorite one yet.

Really great series and all the threads that were set up are coming together. Definitely a little high stress and a bit exhausting where the action and scheming don't let up, but there's a lot of good stuff and interesting exploration of themes and sci-fi concepts.

title: Lonesome Dove
author: Larry McMurtry
review: Masterpiece. One of the best books I've read. Words escape me.

title: Blade of the Immortal, Volume 4: On Silent Wings
author: Hiroaki Samura

title: NOS4A2
author: Joe Hill
review:
Very entertaining and probably my favorite bit of Christmas themed horror that I have read so far. Some great characters and some really dark and messed up stuff that I loved.

I think it could have used some more thematic depth or was missing that extra oomph to tie it all together but I really enjoyed it from beginning to end. Joe Hill's dad does a little bit of a better job fleshing out characters and using a big page count effectively.

Joe Hill is now 2/2 for me and looking forward to reading more of his work.

title: Blade of the Immortal, Volume 5: On Silent Wings II
author: Hiroaki Samura
review: This one was pretty good

title: Us Against You
author: Fredrik Backman
review:
This builds off the first book in the best ways. Some great characters and hard hitting moments. These aren't really standalone and feel like they should be read close together. Really love the town dynamics and the characters get even more depth here.

Backman has some great writing and the themes and foreshadowing kept me really engaged. Felt like I binged this one and had to know what was going to happen.

Much pain, highly recommend.

title: Orcslayer
author: Nathan Long
review: Nathan Long does a great job, excited to continue. This one starts with a 20 year time skip. Very action heavy but some great lore and Dwarf shenanigans.

title: The Winners
author: Fredrik Backman
review:
What a great trilogy with well realized characters and relationships. This one is a bit less focused on the plot but it's great to hang out in Beartown and experience all the pain with the characters. I think I prefer Us Against You a little more but this one is also great.

Backman can hurt you really well in beautiful ways. The ending stretch is absolutely unrelenting and emotionally crushing.

title: Children of Memory
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Tchaikovsky could have just done a similar thing as the last two books with a new alien race and a tiny variation but here he gets weird with it and plays with the concepts of Time (and the Children of...?), Memory, and makes this a surprisingly h(H)uman-centric novel. It's clear he really challenged both himself and the reader which makes for an engaging read, but not often easy. There's also a bit more fantasy elements in this sci-fi and it's not as science based as it was in the previous books.

His writing here is some of his best, prose-wise. There's some great passages and allusions to other works as well as themes that work on multiple levels, but it's also challenging being in the middle of the book and sometimes you feel like you missed something or are confused when it's intentional.

I can see this being a divisive entry in the series, but I personally loved it, although I can see some readers being frustrated with it, seems like a good idea to put this as the third entry to a trilogy for the readers that are already invested in this series and willing to "go on an adventure".

I am very happy to say that he's one of my favorite authors who has astounding productivity and throughput. Highly recommend this series and he's an author that I drop everything to read a new one of his books and have my mind expanded.

title: And Every Morning the Way Home Gets Longer and Longer
author: Fredrik Backman

title: Streets of Laredo
author: Larry McMurtry
review: Not the masterpiece that Lonesome Dove is, but still really good and I enjoyed all my time with this book. Really happy to see some of the character arcs continue from Lonesome Dove and McMurtry is brutal and unforgiving with how he treats these people. Will definitely continue with the other books, some great writing and moments that will stick with me.

title: The Gap Into Ruin: This Day All Gods Die
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
review:
Really liked it overall, thought the climax was great, just some of the retreading wasn't my favorite. Donaldson has the habit of fully fleshing out scenes of characters learning about events that you already knew about which makes it feel a bit bloated.

Some of the writing was really good and he does a great job of bringing the threads together to a satisfying end. Great series if you are interested in sci-fi grimdark, haven't read anything like it before. Of course the content is gruesome especially in the beginning of the series but ends on a hopeful note.

title: Norwegian Wood
author: Haruki Murakami
review:
Japanese Catcher in the Rye for better or worse.

This is a hard book to rate, I did really enjoy a lot of parts of the book but there's definitely some weirdness to it that gets in the way of it being a fully cohesively satisfying novel. Some of the writing was quite good and I got sucked into the slice of life in Japan narrative.

There's quite a bit of weird sex stuff, so yeah, be prepared for that. Some of it I thought added to the narrative / themes and some was borderline disturbing erotica.

Some of the writing captures the human condition really well with the awkwardness, humor, and search for meaning that we all find ourselves in, although as the book went on I felt like the characters actually had less depth. The characters are often very self centered and don't have great healthy relationships with each other which is pretty strange and can come off a little stilted and awkward where it's hard to tell if that's the main character's personality or a shortcoming of the writing.

I do think that I'll enjoy other Murakami books more since this is primarily a romance book and there's not much magical realism to be found.

title: The Golden Compass
author: Philip Pullman
review:
This was ok, I expected more. Lyra bumbles around, gets captured, exposition dump, something happens that's too dark for children, Lyra escapes and somehow ends up where she's supposed to be, repeat. Some interesting world building and sci-fi elements, but I'm not sure if I'm motivated to continue.

Lots of telling over showing and something like Harry Potter which is for similar ages does a lot better job in immersing you in events instead of telling you about what the plot is and why it matters.

title: A Fire Upon the Deep
author: Vernor Vinge
review:
Was sort of hoping for a bit more in either ideas, plot, or characters but there was some good stuff in here. Don't think I'm really chomping at the bit for the next book but maybe in time I will be.

Highlight of the book was probably the different alien races and the world building is very interesting and well thought out. The different zones is a really cool idea, wish it was utilitized a bit more but it made for a good justification for why the universe is set up the way it is.

title: The Shining
author: Stephen King
review: The film is one of my all time favorite horror movies and hadn't read the book before. This shows how great King is with character development, non supernatural horror, and writing about addiction and isolation. The Overlook is hard to beat as one of the best haunted houses, excellent setting that's a character of its own.

title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
author: Jules Verne

title: The Dreaming Void
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review: Couldn't put this down, binged it until I finished. The world building coming off the last series was fantastic and it goes in an interesting and mysterious new direction. I also liked the fantasy POV that a lot of people struggle with.

title: Cardinal Black
author: Robert McCammon
review:
This is a really fun adventure story with some great writing and layers of thematic depth. I was completely engaged from beginning to end and highly recommend the series overall.

There's usually some plot element in these books that make me scratch my head a bit and aren't believable but wasn't too egregious in this one. Looking forward to the next one and at that point I'll be completely caught up with the series.

title: The Temporal Void
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review: Still a good book but definitely the weakest Hammy book I've read so far. Lots of pacing issues and the fantasy sections were way too long and took up way too much of the book. Still really excited to read the final book of the trilogy.

title: The Man From St. Petersburg
author: Ken Follett
review: Solid political thriller and espionage story on the cusp of WW1. Definitely prefer Follet's historical epics but glad to have read this.

title: Vagabond, Vol. 1
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: This was awesome, excited to continue. Great characters, art, and themes. The pacing also turned this into quite the page turner.

title: Vagabond, Vol. 2
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: Never pick a fight with a monk

title: And Put Away Childish Things
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Really interesting and compact Tchaikovsky novella that mixes portal fantasy fairytale with horror and a bit of sci-fi thrown in for spice. I did enjoy the beginning and middle of this quite a bit more than the ending and think it could have been fleshed out a bit more but overall this was really entertaining and quite funny. Definitely a lighthearted read when characters aren't getting brutally impaled.

Tchaikovsky is one of my favorite authors and this really showcases his range, I've read 4 books of his in the past six months and they've all been very different and tackle varying genres and ideas. Highly recommend this one for a fun quick read that subverts existing tropes in entertaining ways.

title: The Evolutionary Void
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review:
This was an awesome sci-fi trilogy. Overall I did like this a little less from a character perspective than Pandora's Star / Judas Unchained but there's still a lot of cool sci-fi moments, action, and technology.

Definitely will dig into more Hammy this year, he's a hit with me and is very consistently good overall.

He's also quite unique within the genre and has a good blend of both old and new sci-fi that is very readable and interesting.

title: Forest Mage
author: Robin Hobb
review:
Incredibly painful, highly recommend. Hobb is my favorite author, Realm of the Elderlings is my favorite series, and the first Soldier Son book I was lukewarm on. Forest Mage has some of her best writing and she's a master at her craft.

So many beautiful and deep passages that work on multiple thematic levels, just some awe inspiring stuff, I highlighted quite a bit. Also she goes in such an unexpected and interesting direction in this book that I really needed after book 1 felt a bit predictable and boring.

This book is quite slow and she takes her time to immerse you in the world and build up the relationships between the characters. Hobb is probably the most skilled at immersing me in her worlds that I have read, you really feel like you are there with Nevare and experiencing his pain.

This book took me a month to read which is pretty slow, but it is heavy and rich and I definitely appreciated it and processed what was going on by taking it slow.

Overall this series doesn't have the most involved plot in the world but Hobb elevates it as a master of her craft, interested to see how this ends and will be reading the rest of her bibliography.

title: Bloodchild and Other Stories
author: Octavia E. Butler
review:
Multiple of these are masterpieces imo. Fantastic set of short stories that do a ton within a short page count.

Deeply rich in themes and subtext that also use sci-fi to its fullest extent to look inward at the human condition, our world around us, and ponder on if it's possible for life to be better and what it means to be human.

Also these are incredibly dark and often bleak that feel like realistic futuristic scenarios. Excited to read more from her, they really resonated with me very well.

title: Ordinary Grace
author: William Kent Krueger
review:
If you haven't read Boy's Life, I'd recommend reading that first since I liked that a lot more, but this was still very good and had a lot of heart. The elements of religion and racism are the big differentiators as well as the events hitting closer to home.

The more I think about the plot though the less I think it's tied up very well and am a bit unsatisfied with how the revelations in the mystery are encountered where in Boy's Life McCammon is the master of plotting and tying things together. I think it's perfectly fair to compare these two because they are so similar but McCammon is also one of my favorite authors so he's hard to match up with.

Overall happy I read this and it had some good emotional moments and beautiful, thoughtful passages. Gets a recommend from me 👍

title: The Long Walk
author: Richard Bachman
review:
