Top tier King for me. It definitely showcases his writing chops in ways his other books don't often do and takes a very simple concept for a plot and elevates it with some amazing characters and pacing.

It's sort of mind blowing that this was written in the 70s before dystopian young adult sci-fi was a thing and it's just as good or better than most stories in the genre.

I'll be thinking about this for a while, captures so much of the beauty, hopelessness, and brutality of being alive.

title: Headtaker
author: David Guymer
review:
Queek is absolutely unhinged, you love to see it.

My expectations for this were really low and it exceeded them greatly. Such a fun book with probably my favorite Warhammer character. So many hilarious Skaven moments and great action sequences between Dwarves, Orcs, and Skaven all fighting in Eight Peaks.

The writing was way better than I thought it would be too and the descriptions of the various locations, battles, and creatures were immersive and interesting.

title: Empire in Black and Gold
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
Really good! I had tempered expectations since this is one of Tchaikovsky's earliest works but the quality of the writing was excellent and at close to the level I've grown to expect from him even when reading his latest releases.

The world building, lore, and history of this series is really interesting so far and there seems to be a lot of depth as well as mystery to uncover and I'm here for it.

Probably one of the most unique series I've read so far. There's bug people! That's really weird and out there, but it makes sense in the world that he's built.

The plot is exciting and the action is well written and easy to visualize. Definitely leans on the side of military fantasy with a lot of assassination attempts, battles, and ambushes. Lots of variety in the action as well with varying races, technology, and unique and interesting locations being fought over.

The characters are also very good and well fleshed out with a lot of complex motivations and morally gray decisions that they are forced to make during war time. I'd have preferred this to maybe be a bit darker but there are some horror elements as well as some meditations on the consequences of violence.

title: A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms
author: George R.R. Martin
series: The Tales of Dunk and Egg, #1-3

title: Under Heaven
author: Guy Gavriel Kay
review:
The prose is probably the best GGK has written so far, some gorgeous passages. The plot in general GGK style is about some of the littler people in larger conflicts who overlap with those in authority positions, I never usually read GGK for the plot and this one is serviceable but not one of his best; the Sarantine Mosaic probably has my favorite plot that he's written.

The characters are pretty good as well and primarily revolves around a single family and the siblings that are spread across the country.

The themes are great and what I come back to GGK for. Some great meditations on mysticism, spirituality, politics, war and power that are integrated well into the narrative.

GGK really cannot be beat in terms of writing beautiful sections that I want to highlight beginning to end.

title: Dawn
author: Octavia E. Butler
review: Great sci-fi horror with really interesting, otherworldly disturbing aliens. Really interested in continuing the series and seeing where Butler goes with this. She really respects your time as a reader and packs a lot into the page count with a lot of compelling ideas and complex characters.

title: Legend
author: David Gemmell
review:
What does it mean to have courage? How do you become and stay a good man? What happens when your Legend has outgrown who you are?

Great heroic fantasy story with a ton of heart that's also deeper than I expected. The writing was good, not flowery but conveyed the story well.

Will definitely be continuing with Drenai and excited to read more from Gemmell.

title: Iron Gold
author: Pierce Brown
review:
Easily my favorite in the series by a large margin. The series really matures and gets a lot darker and more complex.

Adding more POVs made a huge difference. Seeing more of the galaxy and from different perspectives solidifies how cool the world building and the social structure that Brown built way back in the first book.

I was grabbed by the plot and had a hard time putting it down, it took a little bit to establish the new characters and the storylines but my patience was rewarded and there's a lot of great moments and action, along with a lot of surprises.

Really engaging read and Brown's writing has evolved into something special. Most likely jumping right into Dark Age, really want to know what happens, I'm hooked.

title: Dragonfly Falling
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: The bugs must flow. Great book 2. Tchaikovsky challenges and develops the characters really well and places them in difficult situations where they change greatly. The world and lore also reveals further depths. Hyped to continue next month.

title: Adulthood Rites
author: Octavia E. Butler
review: I sort of don't know what to rate this but I think this series is incredible. It is very unique and has some great themes as well as some interesting characters delivered in a compact bleak and dark package. Butler's view of humanity is pretty pessimistic and I love it. However, there's always a sliver of hope.

title: Dark Age
author: Pierce Brown
review: The Storm of Swords of the series and honestly has even more crazy shit happening than even that jam packed book. This was so damn good. A huge roller-coaster from beginning to end. Big climaxes for half a dozen complex storylines and has some shockingly brutally bleak moments. That was intense, yo.

title: Entangled Life: How Fungi Make Our Worlds, Change Our Minds & Shape Our Futures
author: Merlin Sheldrake

title: Imago
author: Octavia E. Butler
review: This one was pretty frustrating. She spent all this time creating good characters, an interesting plot, and deep themes and sort of discarded it all to tell an unrelated story in the same world. Doesn't make sense as the conclusion of the trilogy. I still like and recommend the first two books.

title: Blindsight
author: Peter Watts
review:
The first 75% I really liked and the last 25% I got completely lost and don't think I understood the twists very well or they kind of came out of nowhere. Had some good horror elements and hard sci-fi concepts, did feel a bit let down with the characters a bit and they're really not developed and basically had no attachment to them.

The plot also just sort of starts going and you get almost no backstory about how the world has developed which forces you to read between the lines a lot. I enjoyed this a majority of the time but the end makes me feel like I didn't get it that well or it just wasn't communicated well within the story.

I'm interested in his underwater sci-fi series at some point. I feel like I might not like the sequel to this book but may give it a try eventually.

title: Blood of the Mantis
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
I was sort of mixed for a majority of the book but man, the climax and the way everything was threaded together was awesome. Tchaikovsky continues to build a deeper and more interesting world that has a lot of complexity.

The weak points of the book are that it goes so wide instead of deep with POVs split all across the world and many are brand new locations we've never heard about before. It's sort of a tradeoff because we don't really get as much character development with the existing characters and instead get a grander and more epic setting.

A majority of the book is setting up the conclusion to the final book in the first arc but there's also some good action sequences and tension. Felt like there could have been a little more and I was getting a bit overwhelmed with all the new characters, locations, and factions, but I have a feeling this will pay off for the conclusion of the first arc as well as the 6 other books and all the side books to come.

Really happy to be reading the series and excited to continue. Trust in Tchaikovsky!

title: Vagabond, Vol. 5
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: Incredible, one of the best storylines I've read in a comic.

title: Salute the Dark
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: Really good military and political fantasy with bugs. Satisfyingly wraps up the first arc. Tchaikovsky has built an interesting and complex world that has a lot of directions it could go.

title: The King Beyond the Gate
author: David Gemmell
review: I liked the book and it had a lot of great quotes but it did tread similar ground to Legend. I also was hoping to be more connected to the characters and plot, but still enjoyed it. Will be continuing with Drenai.

title: Light Bringer
author: Pierce Brown
review:
I was lucky enough to get a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. I hate spoilers and this will have none of them. General impressions and vibes below.

Man this was intense. The bar for this book was already incredibly high after loving both Iron Gold and Dark Age being one of the biggest roller coasters since Storm of Swords.

Pierce Brown continues to impress me with his writing growth. We get some of the best imagery in this book that we've had for the whole series. As well as some visceral combat both large and small scale which is hard to do and make it feel tense where anything can happen.

I do think this book has a little bit of inconsistency both within itself and as the larger part of the series. This one is more focused on a smaller number of POVs and goes deeper into the storylines than both Iron Gold and Dark Age.

This can make it so you get less of a well rounded perspective on events and makes it feel closer to the original trilogy than any of the other sequel books so far, however we do get major plot movement and huge things definitely do happen which is great as the penultimate entry in the series. It sets us up for an epic finale as well as respecting everything that came before.

There's also a bit of inconsistency within the book itself where I felt like the highs are very high. There's not really lows, but there are some parts of the book that had less tension or I was hoping tied into the climax a bit more.

Overall I'm really loving the series, was so happy to read an advanced copy of the book, and I'm dying to know how everything ends. Probably my favorite epic political war series since a Song of Ice and Fire with as many twists and jaw dropping moments.

Looking forward to the ending and anything else Pierce Brown writes going forward.

title: Vagabond, Vol. 7
author: Takehiko Inoue
review:
Very compelling read with converging storylines and great characters. There's also a lot of thematic complexity with how samurai are handled and their relation to honor when it comes to the endless cycle of violence and killing.

Even new characters are fleshed out immediately and folded into the narrative. Definitely hooked and want to know what happens next

title: Winter of the World
author: Ken Follett
review:
A fascinating look into how the icy claws of fascism gripped the world prior to WW2 and swept the world into a deadly Winter. I thought I knew a fair bit about WW2 but Follett excels at giving us a view from the ground around the world and how fascism tempted every country and how everyday people fought against it.

It's frightening how relevant this still is and has obvious echoes in modern day that makes one question the nature of humanity.

Maybe my favorite Follett book and I've already read multiple 5 star masterpieces by him. This one does a better job than Fall of Giants at giving you characters to love and hate and builds up masterfully a new set of characters descended from the original cast.

No one does historical generational epics better.

title: The Witchwood Crown
author: Tad Williams
series: The Last King of Osten Ard, #1
review:
No spoilers.

This is a really interesting one. In a lot of ways I feel like *more* should have happened than it did but that really isn't Tad's style and there's a deliberate slow burn as are most of his books.

It feels like a distorted reflection of the Dragonbone Chair and comes perilously close to retreading similar ground but I think this is very intentional and is done so to explore deep themes on the nature of war and humanity.

This is epic fantasy and there's a lot of new POVs, characters, and locations being setup here as well as thirty years since the end of To Green Angel Tower. The world hasn't stood still. Quite the opposite.

There's also a lot of dark things that happen that I'm a fan of. Feels like a more mature and modern Memory Sorrow and Thorn where he doesn't shy away from violent and complex morality.

If Tad executes well on everything he's set up and the promises he's made this will end up being one of the best fantasy series. Taking a little break from the series but wanting this to marinate in my brain a bit before continuing on to Empire of Grass.

title: The Listener
author: Robert McCammon
review: Underread thriller from an underread author. Follows a conman in the south during the depression era. Fans of Stephen King's crime stories will feel right at home. Some brutally poignant moments. A really solid read with exciting moments and nice prose.

title: Berserk Volume 35
author: Kentaro Miura
review: This one was pretty bad and the one before was the best one in a while. Well I'm done with this arc and won't be continuing for a bit until the next arc is finished. Overall the series has been very hit or miss. Some parts have amazing art but the overall story has been a bit disappointing with how few developments there's been.

title: Goodnight Punpun Omnibus, Vol. 2
author: Inio Asano
review: Very dark and depressing, highly recommend!

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Leo Tolstoy
review: Feel like I sort of didn't get it but the writing was pretty readable. Some interesting and often bleak takes on death. Don't think the themes resonated with me as much as I wanted them to. Wasn't that engaged with Ivan's life or able to relate that strongly so maybe that's why I didn't like this as much as I wanted to.

title: They Thirst
author: Robert McCammon
review:
Definitely worth reading and the audiobook narrated by Ray Porter is excellent. I would have preferred if this fleshed out into a book twice as long or a whole series as there was a lot going on and wanted to give some of the characters more important points to contribute towards the resolution of the conflict.

The horror elements are great and McCammon shows how he'd bring great ideas to multiple genres and build unique characters. Also, evil vampires rule.

title: The Crossing
author: Cormac McCarthy
review:
Probably my favorite McCarthy book. The aimlessness and anti climatic tendencies of McCarthy work really well here and give you a lot to think about as there's a lot of thematic complexity in the novel. I keep waffling between a 4 and 5 rating, his books are hard to measure compared to most normal books but I keep coming back for more, so I'm definitely a fan.

Some of it can end up being unsatisfying but that seems like the goal, still getting used to that. Really gorgeous writing and some of the digressions here from the strangers Billy meets through his travels I'll be thinking about for a while.

title: Vagabond, Vol. 12
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: The themes and philosophy are all coming together and give everything that came before so much meaning. Fantastic stuff

title: Vagabond, Volume 37
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: Simply phenomenal

title: Monster: Perfect Edition, Vol. 1
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: Great start to the series, interested to see where this goes and what twists and turns might happen along the way

title: Red Mars
author: Kim Stanley Robinson
review:
Mixed. I really liked the first half of this book and then the length, the direction it was going in, and what it focused on got to me. The characters felt pretty flat and inconsistent to me. Sometimes they were unbearably petty and didn't show much growth or depth, but there were glimpses of some great moments. I didn't really feel much tension in the plot or excited about what was going to happen next.

The science part was probably the highlight, very well researched book and the landscape descriptions were very nice and vivid. Also the terraforming felt based in science and feasible. Some of the other science did seem a bit easy for them to create and not really have ramifications, was hoping for a bit more there. Also showed its age a little bit with how science has advanced since written, but nothing deal breaking there.

title: Parasyte, Volume 1
author: Hitoshi Iwaaki
review: Funny, weird, good art

title: Black Leopard, Red Wolf
author: Marlon James
review:
I only read the first part of this book, but I do feel like it's earned a review warning away everyone from it. This is the most depraved and disgusting book I've read and I don't really feel like there's a deeper meaning to any of it. I've read some very dark books and series but usually they have a point behind the darkness or at least give you moments of reprieve, this book really doesn't and there's some new level of depravity it finds every chapter / page / sentence that is really uncomfortable and is seemingly forgotten in a short amount of time and has no impact on the characters and setting.

Nicest thing I can say about this book is I thought the writing at points was quite good and there were some weird dreamlike sequences that were interesting.

I don't know, maybe I don't get it, but I feel like as an enjoyer of dark weird books if I don't really like this book I'd want to heavily discourage anyone else from reading it.

title: Empire of Grass
author: Tad Williams
series: The Last King of Osten Ard, #2
review: Fantastic, top tier fantasy. So much good stuff and complex storylines intertwining. Osten Ard is a beautiful, lush, and rich place steeped in deep lore that has a lot of mystery and danger. Some of the best stuff I've read since ASOIAF.

title: At the Mountains of Madness
author: H.P. Lovecraft
review: 3.5/5 rounded up because Keeble does a Boston accent in the audiobook. Cool creature history and lore.

title: Naoki Urasawa's Monster, Volume 4
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: Getting more complex and also more interesting. Great side characters and still a lot of mystery with more layers being unveiled as we go.

title: The Road to Jerusalem
author: Jan Guillou
review:
Definitely a bit of a setup book but interested in where the series goes. Book is fairly zoomed out and a bit of a history book at times that can make it feel impersonal but it also gives you more context of the historical period it takes place in.

This is pre Crusading but there's compelling thoughts on the contradiction of religion that preaches love and crusading against non believers and how the standards for masculinity are vastly different from what we know today. Also good stuff on how actual medieval Swedish settlements were run and the varying standards of food and drink have changed.

title: Monster Perfect Edition 5
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: Character work and plot continue being phenomenal

title: Naoki Urasawa's Monster, Volume 6
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: The Monster inside me keeps growing and growing!

title: The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo
author: Stieg Larsson
review:
I'd watched both the American and Swedish adaptions of this book a number of years ago but have forgotten most about them aside from the larger strokes. Really enjoyed the mystery in this one and the process of solving it.

The falling action was pretty strange and felt like it should have been in the next book is my only complaint.

Lizbeth is an all timer character, Mikael is sort of interesting as well but harder to pin down his motivations. Loved the setting and the family dynamics were really complex and intricate.

Will definitely continue with book 2 in the near future.

title: Into the Narrowdark
author: Tad Williams
review:
This series is simply phenomenal and I didn't want this book to end. I want to read the next one right now! The intertwining storylines are done the best here since A Song of Ice and Fire. Definitely one of my highlights of the year.

If I have any shred of criticism it is that it does feel like the penultimate book of the series and we don't get things wrapped up here at all, but it runs with the events of Grass really well.

Tad is vastly under appreciated and hope with this series being completed more people pick these up!

title: The Templar Knight: An Epic Medieval Adventure of Faith and War in the Holy Land
author: Jan Guillou

title: Manslayer
author: Nathan Long
review:
Definitely the weakest plot in the series so far, but still having a lot of fun with the series and the audiobooks read by Jonathan Keeble are fantastic.

Also very happy with Nathan Long continuing the series, just wish Gotrek and Felix had more interesting stuff to do in this one. Some good returning characters and get a good look at the Empire from the inside.

title: The Reality Dysfunction
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review:
It says a lot that I finished a book 1 that clocks in at 1200 pages and want to pick up the next book immediately. This book is big, bold, complex, dense, and unapologetically dark; like really dark man. Would call this sci-fi horror easily since the darkness and disturbing events are so pervasive. As a fan of dark horror books, really liked this aspect and we don't see it enough in sci-fi.

Peter F Hamilton is cemented as one of my favorite sci-fi authors after loving his Commonwealth Saga series. He continues to impress with his unique blend of sci-fi that balances ideas, characters, technology, and vivid worlds - among many other things.

Also, even though I'd classify this as a space opera and the scale is indeed big, we do get a lot of page time on a single planet which is refreshing for the genre as we get a lot of time experiencing the richness of this one world and the people, the aliens, and the strange wildlife that lives there.

This book is also really weird and isn't afraid to have crazy stuff happen. There's a lot of mystery for why this weird stuff is happening and there seems to be some unrevealed logic to why these things are happening.

I don't think I'd recommend this book to most people, but if you're brave enough to commit to these giant tomes he writes you'll be rewarded with a very rich and interesting portal into one of sci-fi's greatest imaginations.

The book also seemed to fly by and I was always interested in what was going to happen next, the pacing is very good and never felt like any part really overstayed its welcome. Lots of POVs that all feel distinct and interesting.

I honestly have no idea where this series is going to go, but I have some tinfoil hat theories and excited to continue and experience the ride.

title: Killers of the Flower Moon: The Osage Murders and the Birth of the FBI
author: David Grann
review:
3.5/5 the content of the book was definitely interesting but felt like it could have been told in a more engaging way at times.

Anticipating the film coming out this month, I think Scorsese will adapt this in a more dramatized, compelling way.

Definitely a very dark string of murders and conspiracy. This book also felt a little too short and you don't really end up feeling connected with many of the victims and instead the investigators end up getting more of the spotlight.

I did enjoy the look into Hoover and some of the early days of the FBI, I previously didn't know that much about it and thought that aspect was really interesting and I want to learn more about it.

The amount of lawlessness and corruption is really disturbing but makes a compelling read especially in the context of bringing law and order to the frontier of the west and how that affects the native people living there. Reality can be stranger than fiction so I appreciated the presentation of the facts here even though it could come off a bit dry at times.

title: One Piece, Vol. 5: For Whom the Bell Tolls
author: Eiichiro Oda

title: One Piece, Vol. 4: The Black Cat Pirates
author: Eiichiro Oda

title: The Stand
author: Stephen King
review:
A flawed masterpiece. Has some of the highest highs from one of my favorite authors and the lows aren't as bad as I've heard, I was bracing myself for a way worse ending and ended up pleasantly surprised.

The first 60 percent or so is definitely a lot stronger, but also found some really good moments in the rest of the book. I do think this book requires a lot of suspension of disbelief and it works better when you're riding the wave of the slice of life moments instead of trying to think critically on if the plot logically fits together as a whole.

This has been on my bucket list reads for ages and am very happy I read it.

title: Sandkings
author: George R.R. Martin
review: Read this and a few other GRRM horror short stories and really liked them

title: Let Me In
author: John Ajvide Lindqvist
review: Visceral, uncomfortable, and disturbing. Feels like a realistic take on what would actually happen if vampires existed. Great small town dynamics and complex characters that have varied motivations. Tackles a lot of uncomfortable topics head on that I imagine will be off putting to a lot of people.

title: The Neutronium Alchemist
author: Peter F. Hamilton
review:
Honestly sort of struggled with this one. It also feels like such a middle book where the beginning is a lot of climax and falling action before introducing the main drive for this book. And nothing is really resolved after 1200 pages which can feel a bit unrewarding even though there's a lot of good stuff in between.

The main plot point I did struggle to get motivated by or at least the moment to moment parts were less interesting than the first book, but the drives behind it and the potential consequences are very high.

The horror elements felt a lot less prevalent here as well which I sort of view as a negative since I really enjoyed that in the first book and was missing those here.

The amount of plot lines and the complexity of the world and events almost hit a breaking point for me, but it barely holds things together here and we do get some really good moments and some of the characters we've been interacting with have interesting and high consequence things to do.

There's also a lot of complexity in the motivations and the different factions where even the main protagonist and antagonist factions have many different sub factions who have different motivations and objectives.

Overall this is a lot of book and can feel overwhelming a lot of times but it's also really good and so much is left unanswered that I do want to know how PFH wraps it all up.

Pretty impressed as well how this maintains the brand of big bold and unforgiving science fiction but in a drastically different way from the previous book. Makes it easy to respect the sheer will and ambition of the series even though it can feel like drowning at times.

Will take a bit of a breather before I slowly digest the last book and see what's in store for this crazy universe this man has crafted.

title: The Passing of the Dragon
author: Ken Liu
review: A bit too on the nose for me and tries to do too much with its short page count. I'm a huge fan of Liu's other work but this was a miss for me. Having a story be about contemporary online art criticism really doesn't resonate with me unfortunately.

title: Doctor Sleep
author: Stephen King
review: Had a good time with this one, not King's absolute best but think it serves as an interesting continuation of the story. King is one of the best at making long time period coming of age feel authentic and this is no exception. Had some great themes to investigate and diving even deeper into King's magic system was fun as it has implications across his multiverse of stories and this has been the most direct look into it that I've seen across his books that I've read. Also had really good thriller aspects that kept me engaged and wanting to know what would happen next.

title: Solaris
author: Stanisław Lem
review:
**spoiler alert** I was sort of hoping that the book would build more and more on the horror elements but in many ways the focus of this was the love story between Kelvin and Harey which I didn't expect and was a bit strange for me. I don't think I fully bought into the why aspect of this but there was a lot of struggle internally with Kelvin and a lot of ways he was the most unreasonable character and everyone else on the station tries to make him snap out of it (even Harey)

I did like the philosophy towards the end about whether God is a clock maker but didn't create time and relating that to some of the impossibility of understanding something completely alien.

The tangents into some of the in world books and science I was sort of eh on and felt like similarly with Lovecraft there's a lot of rumination that sort of makes the pacing of the story stumble a bit

Overall pretty solid book

title: A Wizard of Earthsea
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review:
There's beauty in simplicity. Seemingly simple words strung together in a way that can evoke vivid visuals and explore deep and complex themes. The story is also fairly simple but covers a huge amount of ground and is able to explore a huge number of relationships, events, and evolution in Ged's life. The world is rich and detailed without Le Guin really spending a huge amount of time explaining things; instead the reader explores the world with Ged and learns alongside him.

I also think the story is unique and Le Guin delves into a lot of the motivation in the afterward as well and how she's able to do that without having war and violence be at the center of the novel (although Ged straight up kills a couple of people lol). Also didn't really feel like this was focused on pandering to teens and it feels like a fully adult novel, just has a character that is coming of age throughout the story but it deals with weighty themes and confronts the reader with big questions about humanity and our place in it relative to nature, among many other things.

Wasn't really expecting to love this as much as I did, I read the Dispossessed a few years ago and it was very pulled back prose-wise in order to make the politics the center of the novel, this book has no such qualms. Le Guin is only operating in the constraints where she wants the novel to be accessible to a large number of readers, but the language is often strikingly beautiful and vivid. There are some complex sections as well and she doesn't hold back on the world being grand in scale and having a lot of mystery.

title: The Tombs of Atuan
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: The atmosphere in this book was incredible and the prose is top notch. I do feel like I wanted a tad more complexity in the plot or characters to push this to five stars but still had a great time reading this. Le Guin gives me a lot to think about, her themes are very complex.

title: The Scarab Path
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
This might be the best one yet, a lot of payoff on lore and character arcs that have been building up in the previous books in a cool new setting. Also think Tchaikovsky's prose was really nice in this one, had a lot of passages I wanted to highlight and think about.

The series is very military and action focused which at times I feel like I can get fatigued about it but overall the action is very cool and well written.

Looking forward to the next one quite a bit, back on the bugbook train, bugman take the wheel!

title: The Dregs of Empire
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
I really liked this a lot. Great side story that had really good pacing. Somehow Ruocchio's writing gets better every book and he was already one of the best, this one was really balanced with great prose, impactful character moments, and the plot is also very clear and focused.

Lorian is such a great character and getting to know him well in this book should payoff in future books as well as enhance re-reads tremendously. I'll be unclear how essential this book will be until I read Disquiet Gods but it's definitely worth anyone's time who has read through Ashes of Man.

title: The Dead Zone
author: Stephen King
review:
This was solid, definitely very far from my favorite King but I was entertained and glad I read it.

The parts were better than the sum for me, it felt like a slightly disjointed book and wasn't tied together as much as I wanted. Felt like it had concepts for multiple different books that didn't quite fit together and the beginning is very different from the end.

I do think I read this at a good time as I've read some of the big King books he's written both prior to and after the Dead Zone and this one sort of sits between a few others in King's multiverse.

Which for that alone I'm glad to have read it as you can see a lot of DNA here for future (and better) King books.

title: Tales of the Sun Eater, Volume 3
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review: Every one of these stories were damn good and expanded the world and lore in really cool ways. Also had some awesome action sequences. Definitely think a couple of these are critical before Disquiet Gods, some really big revelations and teasers for the next book. Big HYPE

title: The Reversal
author: Michael Connelly
series: The Lincoln Lawyer, #3; Harry Bosch Universe, #22
review: Really close to a 5 star read but was hoping to see sort of a different ending. Everything leading up to it was great though. Connelly's attention to detail in both the investigation and trial makes the book feel realistic and engaging. Loved the team up and utilizes the strong characters he's built up in previous books.

title: Real, Vol. 2
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: I'm ready to get hurt again

title: Elfslayer
author: Nathan Long
review: Maybe the coolest plot so far, this was awesome

title: The Justice of Kings
author: Richard Swan
review:
I've been wanting to read this book for some time and had high expectations for it. It's met and exceeded them. Now that book 3 is almost out it was a good time to begin the trilogy.

Loved the core mystery of the book, the horror elements, and the zoomed-in feeling that soaked in the atmosphere and made the violence very visceral and high stakes.

The characters were also fantastic and had interesting backstories that were quickly told and the pacing of the whole book was perfect, definitely wanted to keep reading and see what would happen next. Excited to read the rest of the trilogy very soon.

title: Real, Vol. 4
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: The themes in this are incredible. Love the meditation on how we push others away and isolate ourselves while when we let people in and become a part of a community we can have different purposes in life we never expected. Heavy and (Real) beautiful stuff.

title: Real, Vol. 7
author: Takehiko Inoue
review: The themes, characters, and action in this series is fantastic. Top tier sports story.

title: Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones
author: James Clear

title: The Last Coyote
author: Michael Connelly
review: Loved this one from beginning to end. Great Bosch backstory and an interesting case with a lot of twists and turns. Really kept me guessing and the way everything came together was masterful.

title: Seven Shades of Evil
author: Robert McCammon
review: Great collection of well plotted and entertaining short stories with brilliant writing. McCammon is my guy!! None are absolutely essential to the overall plot of the series but we do get some good moments with characters we don't regularly see in the main series as well as go a little bit outside the lines and have some fun with different types of stories.

title: The Trials of Empire
author: Richard Swan
review:
I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

Man this trilogy rocks. I've been patiently waiting to start it until the release of the third book was in sight and here we are at the end of a satisfying conclusion for the Empire of the Wolf.

This is definitely fantasy horror, more so than the previous two books which had horror elements but less pervasive than this one. I'm personally a horror fan so I loved the inclusion of the horror and visceral violence in this book. I think sci-fi and fantasy needs more of it.

I have a hard time ranking the three books in this trilogy as I feel like they're consistently good but also fairly distinct from one another. This one has a bit more focus with the finish line in sight and a clear resolution to wrap things up which means a lot less side stories but it still holds a number of surprises.

I think if you liked the previous two books you'll like this one and if you haven't you'll like these if you want a good blend of interesting, morally gray characters, supernatural horror, and great combat and battle scenes along with some mystery.

Overall this trilogy has been one of the highlights of my reading year and I highly recommend reading them.

title: The Return of Nagash
author: Joshua Reynolds
review: Super fun audiobook. Probably the largest scale Warhammer book I've read so far. Lots of great races and faction interactions including legendary characters and higher stakes. Probably a bit too large and a bit too much stabby stabby going on and needs a bit of breathing room, but a lot of cool stuff happens.

title: The Poet
author: Michael Connelly
review:
On a Connelly hot streak, been loving his work lately. This one had more elevated prose in it, especially the beginning really sucked me in and had a great premise with realistic characters and taking place in Denver felt like a nice breath of fresh air.

The plot was pretty much perfect and kept me guessing, had a lot of twists and turns and the details mattered a lot. Highly recommend this one and think it'd also make a good entry point to his work in general, doesn't require any previous books.

title: The Farthest Shore
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review:
Gorgeous book with a ton of thematic depth. The series feels very mythological in a way, where what is gained from the story are the metaphors we draw from it and how we can apply it to our lives. Definitely some of the best prose I've read, flows really well and lots of great passages to reflect on. I did appreciate some of the darkness that contrasts with the light and beauty we see.

"He has done with doing. He goes home."

title: The Sea Watch
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: Probably my favorite one so far. Everything Tchaikovsky built up in previous books reaps a lot of rewards here with the world building, politics, characters while he expands the scope in interesting ways. Some beautiful visuals in this one too. Looking forward to the next book even though everyone I know hates it

title: The Green Mile
author: Stephen King
review: I'm not crying, you're crying. King and prisons, name a better combo. Just amazing character work. I definitely am rewatching the movie after this!

title: Tehanu
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review:
Honestly not sure what to rate this, don't take my rating too seriously

Definitely glad I read the book even though it was sort of a bleak tough read with a lot of anger and fear towards how our society (and the society of Earthsea) is structured and the power imbalances that arise from this structure.

After the previous books being epic and mythological this book is very grounded and mundane, it's also the darkest one yet and there's quite a lot of "sociological horror" surrounding what it's like to be a woman, child, or the poor in this society and how grim the prospects really are in these circumstances.

However there's still moments of beauty and light. I did find this as an interesting meditation on what it's like to be past your prime and aging and thinking about what happens when you feel inadequate and fixating on past failures.

Le Guin really gives me a lot to think about and I think I'll sit on this one for a while and digest it a bit before continuing to her short stories but I always find something in her works to ponder deeply. She definitely has a lot of wisdom and has some great ideas about a large swath of themes and topics.

This sort of feels like a sister novel to Left Hand of Darkness even though I haven't read it, but makes me more interested in what she has to say about gender in her other works.

title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
author: Philip K. Dick
review:
**spoiler alert** I do think PKD plots leave me a bit unsatisfied but with Ubik at least I felt like it's grown on me and needed to be digested a bit as sort of a mental time bomb

The scene that stuck out to me the most was the android snipping off the spider's legs, that was fucked up and they ended up being pretty messed up even laughing that they may have killed the last spider on earth.

Isidore was a pretty sympathetic character and it was also hard to tell whether he was reacting to the inhumanity of the androids or his mental impairment really caused him to act pretty inconsistently but he was an interesting POV to analyze how empathy looked between humans and androids.

I have no idea what the Mercer plot line is supposed to mean, that was pretty trippy and also I didn't understand it 😂

title: Shamanslayer
author: Nathan Long
review: Had fun with this one. Sort of felt like a bit of a side quest but we got a lot of cool Beastmen lore and even some character development! Woah! As always has some amusing dialogue and Keeble is the goat narrator so the audiobook is an absolute treat.

title: Real, Vol. 15
author: Takehiko Inoue
review:
This series has been a bit up and down for me but this latest volume was fantastic. The themes it deals with are frustration and failure so it can be a bit hard to read sometimes because it ends up being frustrating since it can feel like not a lot of progress is made in the story. I was honestly pretty close to souring on the series but this volume reminded me of all the things I love in it.

However the latest volume gives me a lot of hope that when the series continues that things will pick up and start anew.

The series is at its best when it deals with the trauma of the characters and their motivations when they face adversity.

Inoue has this habit of absolutely crushing the last released volumes of his manga and hitting hard with deep impactful themes. I felt similarly about the ending of Vagabond and its takeaways about community and the vulnerability of asking for help and this volume of Real hit on similar levels.

title: Disquiet Gods
author: Christopher Ruocchio
review:
July 2025 review:
Yes this continues to be one of my favorite books. Both insanely rich but also incredibly well paced. Having some of the series details fresher makes this even more rewarding. So ready to read Shadows Upon Time.

January 2024 review:
Masterpiece. This is why I read. If you're not reading this series what are you doing?

Howling Dark was my favorite Sun Eater book yet and this is twice as good and has the craziness dialed up to 11. The prose is immaculate, the politics complex, the horror utterly terrifying and deeply disturbing, the strange is otherworldly and mind expanding.

Only sad thing is that this is probably going to be the best book I've read all year and I have to wait for Ruocchio's next book.

This feels like both the most unique entry yet but also distinctly Sun Eater and walks a high wire teetering on the edge of disaster that somehow holds it all together and is immensely satisfying, surprising, and rewarding for what has been teased before, and what is promised after.

I shall go on alone.

title: Lord Foul's Bane
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
series: The Chronicles of Thomas Covenant the Unbeliever, #1
review:
"Hellfire! Don't touch me, I'm a leper!". Thomas Covenant is one of the most petulant, cowardly, and reluctant protagonists you'll meet.

A lot of this book feels heavily inspired by Lord of the rings, at a point that I feel like how similar it is must be intentional and trying to offer some commentary by having such an unlikable protagonist in a fairly vanilla fantasy world.

The book is also much longer than the page count indicates and also feels very long and can be dense with the lore and the word choice in the prose. The pace is also pretty slow, Donaldson has a habit of rehashing the plot every few chapters.

I did like the world of the Land and the scenery descriptions were often nice and immersive.

This book is in a weird point in time between classical quest fantasy and more modern works where it feels like the grandfather of grimdark with a pinky toe into some of those ideas but the characters can feel fairly flat and not that complex.

Overall pretty mixed on this. I do think the central mystery is compelling but also the plot beats and the characters I was hoping to be much stronger.

The foundation of the book and world does seem fairly solid so with more interesting plot and characters I could see this getting better as the series continues.

Will give book 2 a shot and hope it improves.

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 1
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: Really good start. Great action, interesting characters, and the themes it hinted at exploring all have me eager to continue. Some minor anime tropes here but they kind of add some additional flavor to the Viking story.

title: Mine
author: Robert McCammon
review: 3.5/5 I do have some plot criticisms. The prose was great as per usual for RMC. Fairly standard thriller but some interesting elements and the character of Mary was absolutely unhinged but wish we had a bit more depth overall in some of the characters. Glad I read this overall.

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 2
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: Love it. Feels sufficiently different from other viking stories that I don't feel burned out and a lot of great themes and complexity here with some dark things happening. Really interested to see where this goes.

title: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
author: J.K. Rowling
review: This series has really flown under the radar, but I can see it getting popular someday!

title: Zombieslayer
author: Nathan Long
review: This one was slow and shambling like a zombie unfortunately. Maybe more like a 2.5/5 but not by much.

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 4
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: Holy shit!

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 5
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: What a great series. Definitely a lot different from the previous volume but great themes and philosophy

title: God Emperor of Dune
author: Frank Herbert
review:
I attempted this one about 15 years ago and glad I gave it another shot. Really liked the themes and philosophy.

The scale of this one is also surprisingly small and the most common scene is two characters talking to each-other in a room, not a lot of action but liked a lot of the subtlety and nuance between the character relationships even though the character writing is a bit dry as it was in previous books.

The series goes in really cool directions and I absolutely love the world-building done, feels like a very rich, expansive universe with a lot of potential.

Planning on continuing and finally finishing up this series for the first time.

title: The Illearth War
author: Stephen R. Donaldson
series: The Chronicles of Thomas Covenant the Unbeliever, #2
review: DNF 45% Donaldson failed to make me care about the Land or anyone in it in 1.5 books, I'm done

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 7
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: First half was amazingly good, not sure how I feel about the second but interested to see where the story goes from here

title: The Fall
author: Ryan Cahill
review:
Just what I needed: to enjoy another big unfinished fantasy series! Feels like a climax to a book you haven't read.

The action was quite fun and really liked the high magic aspects and the dragon fights were very cool. The writing is far from flowery but felt very clear on what was happening and has some nice environment descriptions that were efficient.

The world seems cool and interested to learn more about some of these factions and the people in them.

Definitely interested to pick up the first book and this was a great idea by Cahill as a sampler before going full bore into a big first book and series.

title: Of Blood and Fire
author: Ryan Cahill
review:
Familiar and comfortable. And a bit cozy at times which was nice. Had some good action and planted the seeds for future character development. The magic usage is also pretty cool and not overly explained. I do wish some of the races and creatures had a bit more meat to them.

Took a bit to get going and compared with The Fall I definitely enjoyed this less and it stumbled a bit in places but not majorly, could definitely just tell this was Cahill's first book.

Definitely showed some promise for future books. The world building is fairly vanilla which can be something that really elevates book 1s for me but fairly standard fantasy fare.

I do think this series will hinge on the characters and how it explores both sides of this conflict, some of the antagonist POVs are particularly good even though we don't get a lot of them.

This was easy to read and I did find myself really wanting to pick it back up again and again which is a good sign. I've already started book 2 as well which is a good endorsement, I want to see where this goes and if it hits the level of The Fall in the main novels.

title: Of Darkness and Light
author: Ryan Cahill
review:
Huge step up from book one, exponentially better. And I liked book 1! Had a great time with this one and loved the epic scale, the characters, and action.

Sets up some really cool stuff for the next book and has a lot of great moments.

A couple of stumbles along the way mainly with some dialogue and some of the prose being a little awkward still but not as frequent as book 1. Also a couple of the storylines were much weaker than the rest, but all of them definitely have moments where they shine so not suffering through it by any stretch.

Definitely a fun series that takes what makes fantasy great, doesn't do anything too crazy with it but ends up being a satisfying and engaging read. I think Cahill will get even better as he gets more experience.

title: Trunk Music
author: Michael Connelly
review:
definitely a good one, probably liked a little bit less than the last few Connelly books I've read but still really good

The plot kept me guessing and had a satisfying conclusion. Didn't really resonate on themes or attempt anything that deep here but a fun mystery and adventure for our hero Detective Bosch.

title: Revelation Space
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
This was awesome. Felt satisfied with the ending and there's a lot more of the series left which I'm excited to read. Really great balance of mind blowing ideas, cool plot, and interesting world building. Reynolds is probably my favorite space opera author and this might be my favorite book of his I've read so far.

Sort of feel similarly towards this as I do Three Body Problem where I don't think it's for everyone and some people will bounce off of it hard but for me personally it's right up my alley. It's also very technical at times and you can tell it was written by an astrophysicist, but I loved this aspect and feels very grounded in real science but expanded in a huge way to explore big ideas.

The characters and exposition dumps are probably the weak parts but some of this can sort of be handwaved away by the amount of post humanism the characters have undergone.

Pretty hooked by this and eager to read Chasm City SOOOON

title: Chasm City
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
Pretty invested in the series now that this one also blew me away and is also quite different from Revelation Space. So he's now 2/2 for the Revelation Space series and I've really enjoyed the standalones of his that I've read. Shows the range of Reynolds well.

The way things clicked together by the end was really impressive and well planned out. You do sort of have to trust the author in the beginning and there can be some confusing elements to the story but by the end it's very clear why it is told this way.

Only some minor flaws here with some of the plotting and side characters, but was engaged with this from beginning to end.

The scope ended up being a lot bigger than I thought and still tackled some expansive sci-fi ideas well fleshing out the already excellent world building from the first book.

The environments, cityscapes, and straight up weird stuff in this one was really good and unique. Planning to read the whole series as well as the optional side novellas / short stories, haven't been this hot on a sci-fi series in a while, definitely has what I'm looking for in the genre as well as incorporating dark and fantastic and dark elements from horror.

title: Vinland Saga Omnibus, Vol. 11
author: Makoto Yukimura
review: This series sort of lost me, don't know if I'll finish it

title: Diamond Dogs, Turquoise Days
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
3.5/5 so I did really like this but sort of rating it against the enjoyment and satisfaction I had with Revelation Space & Chasm City it's definitely below those both by a fair bit. Did get some interesting stories with quite different flavors from anything I've read from Reynolds so far and some world building that should be helpful to know when continuing the main series.

I do think the mysteries and reveals aren't as good as the main books, maybe due to page count, maybe not. It does overall provide me with more questions than answers about the universe of this world.

Would probably say that these are skippable but maybe my opinion will change after reading more books in the series but glad I read them and they're roughly of equal quality to each-other with maybe a slight preference for the plot of Diamond Dogs.

title: Heirs of the Blade
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review:
This was just ok. My expectations were sufficiently in check too since a lot of people I've been reading this series with said this was probably the worst book.

Definitely a bit of a bummer after loving the last two books but there's some good stuff here. Just the main focus of the book follows a character that I don't really enjoy and her motivations are pretty perplexing and not particularly well done.

I do like the tendency of these books of going darker and more complex plot lines, and I also think the prose keeps getting better, some nice passages in the book.

This is probably the most middle book in the series but some of the follow on stuff from Scarab Path and the setup for the last trilogy is some of the best stuff in this one so I feel optimistic about the final trilogy of books.

title: The Balkans: A Captivating Guide to the History of the Balkan Peninsula, Starting from Classical Antiquity through the Middle Ages to the Modern Period
author: Captivating History

title: Redemption Ark
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
This definitely has some flaws but the amount of cool stuff in it makes it a great read and I'm happy I spent most of my reading time this month on it.

I do prefer the intricate mystery puzzle box of Revelation Space and Chasm City to the style of this book where it's more plot centric and getting from A to B, however Reynolds does flesh out one of the factions in a really interesting and well done way as well as develop the characters a bit better than Revelation Space.

I do sort of feel like the overall plan for the series isn't as planned out as individual books and some parts were seemingly glossed over and skipped while characters later fill us in on what happened and I don't like that way of storytelling.

If I could have Reynolds re-write this book before releasing I think it needed a lot more pages to fully flesh everything out in a way I'd find completely satisfying. I'm not sure if there was publisher pressure to keep it shorter but it's something I noticed.

Compared to someone like Peter F Hamilton who has these massive books where some things probably should have been cut out, this feels like the opposite problem. I can sort of fill in the gaps mentally but I think it'd make the book a lot more satisfying in the end.

However we do get big cool sci-fi ideas and there's a lot of nuance in the factions that feels very realistic to me and even for alien races or advanced humans, there's a lot of infighting and differences of opinion that can lead to violence.

The theme of redemption is also explored but I do wish it was a bit more subtle as some of the characters do talk about it explicitly a few times and that makes it not land as well for me. Also some of the character actions don't really feel consistent with who they are for me which can make it feel less believable, sometimes it feels like it's just to serve the plot.

Interested to see where the series goes but taking a little breather from the series before continuing. It doesn't feel as planned out as I thought after finishing the other books but I enjoy my time in this universe.

title: The Navigator's Children
author: Tad Williams
review:
4.5/5

No spoilers or any mention of any plot points in any of the books, only high level thoughts on this book and the series as a whole are in this review.

Thank you to DAW books and Netgalley for this early copy. I received a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

The main plot ended on a very satisfying and exciting climax, probably one of the biggest and best stretches of action in any Tad Williams book that I've read. The complexity of the lore that has always been present but is just now being revealed is incredible. Like an intricate puzzle box hiding deep secrets in plain sight, it'll be interesting to re-read the series in the future now that we know some of the big answers to the questions that have been asked years ago.

The mysteries in this series are great. I do think a couple of the mysteries didn't have as satisfying of a resolution and were a little simple with not much payoff, but one of the big main ones, wow, I've been thinking about had so many big moments of payoff in this book that I could barely put the book down and stop reading.

The prose is incredible and some of the best in the fantasy genre, period. Tad writes in such a visual, evocative way that blends the surreal and fantastical in ways that also hits a lot of emotion, just superb. Honestly I expect this from him at this point after the whole series has had gorgeous writing and it doesn't disappoint here.

Some of the side stories I do wish had more complex resolutions or were folded into the main plot better and had some pretty straightforward resolutions that were a little disappointing considering how much the build up was throughout the series. I'm not sure why this happened but I feel like A Song of Ice and Fire did this considerably better but some of the plots were wrapped up a bit too neatly where I do like more messy resolutions with a lot of things going wrong and in unexpected directions.

I did feel satisfied with a lot of the character arcs, but also some of them I wish had a little more complexity in the resolutions and in some ways I think another trilogy will be needed to make it completely satisfying which is a bit unfortunate.

I loved a lot of the moral and political complexity here and the sequel series overall does a lot better in this aspect than Memory, Sorrow, Thorn. We get a lot of great perspectives from non human characters and get to grapple with their inhuman value systems and their differing political structures.

Overall Tad is one of the best authors currently writing fantasy and the bar for this book and my expectations were sky high and this mostly delivers in a satisfying way.

I love the world of Osten Ard and will happily return when Tad writes more books in the world, and I'm also expecting this will be the case. There are a few novellas already in the works but I also expect another trilogy will be possible in the future.

Highly recommend the series and was so happy to read this early and be able to take my time immersing myself in this world.

My standards were insanely high and I'll be thinking about this series and world for a long time to come. I've re-read the original series right before continuing with Last King of Osten Ard and I can see myself easily re-reading everything again in the future.

title: Raft
author: Stephen Baxter
review:
Really good old man sci-fi with cool ideas and some unexpected darkness in a few unique settings. Yes the characters are a little bit cardboard but I think they're serviceable. If this is the worst one in the series I'm excited to continue.

Someone recommended this to people who loved the Three Body Problem series and for the most part I do agree. The science does seem to be reasonably realistic to me but also is there to make a good story and explore humanity in interesting ways.

The sociological aspects were quite good and it avoids the pitfalls in some older sci-fi where humans are mostly smart and rational where here we do see panicked groups and cruelty between different groups of society that is recognizably human.

There might be a couple of gaps in the science but they're easy to overlook in order to get cool ideas going.

The pacing was also pretty good and the book was pretty consistent. I do think it peaked a bit in the middle with a couple of awesome chapters but there's also a number of cool moments throughout the book. This really put my imagination to the test and had some interesting ideas to think about.

title: Timelike Infinity
author: Stephen Baxter
review:
This book is wild. So many "holy shit" moments from the crazy ideas. A big upgrade over Raft. The characters are also a lot better even though they're not the focus. Small book that packs a big punch and wastes no time getting to the good stuff. The writing also seems a bit better and I was highlighting quite a few passages.

Excited to continue the series.

title: Dungeon Crawler Carl
author: Matt Dinniman
review: 3.5/5 the audiobook performance is indeed amazing and I liked the humor, definitely will check out book 2! It definitely got better as it went, the rpg stuff in the beginning was a bit distracting and detracted from the story a bit.

title: Carl's Doomsday Scenario
author: Matt Dinniman
review: The plot really went off the rails on this one and the momentum of the second half of book 1 felt lost here. Lots of side quests I don't really care about. Don't think I'll be continuing.

title: Needful Things
author: Stephen King
review:
Man, this rocked. Very underread King novel that plays to his strengths in big ways. I do have a couple of nitpicks and ideally would have been even longer and even more fleshed out but the small town dynamics are hugely impressive.

King just gets you to care about characters so fast and the back stories and histories of these ordinary people are so well done and interesting. The way their lives are interweaved makes for a feeling of epic scale in a small place.

Also some absolutely horrifying and disturbing moments, even for a King book and a lot of things that are implied that aren't shown that will stick with me and have me thinking about it. There's a lot to latch onto here in this small but busy town with a lot of angles to approach the story and I imagine different storylines will stick with people differently, even some of the smaller plot lines have a lot of power in a small amount of page time.

The themes are well crafted and timeless, this one aged really well, highly recommend a read through this and it makes me excited to read Under the Dome in a strange way to get those town dynamics again in another massive tome of a novel.

title: Absolution Gap
author: Alastair Reynolds
review:
This one has really bad reviews online but I actually liked it quite a bit. Definitely a bit of a slower burn than others in the series and genre but the reveals and climax are exciting and interesting. I think the negative reception could be because this sort of is unconventional approach to a finale in the space opera genre and the story isn't what I would've expected after finishing the first book.

The character development and arcs are all quite good overall and we get satisfying conclusions to a lot of character's stories that are big differences from where they started.

The atmosphere of the settings is also well done and unique. We get some 40k reminiscent settings, eldritch horror, and even tropical and tundra type settings that feel very unique and well described. I could picture the settings and cool events happening pretty easily due to Reynolds descriptions.

Excited to read the rest of the series as well as the Prefect books soon.

title: Angels Flight
author: Michael Connelly
review: This went to crazy and unexpected places from a fairly standard beginning, really enjoyed it

title: Pilgrim: A Medieval Horror
author: Mitchell Lüthi
review:
The parts were better than the sum. Kind of tough to review but it never really grabbed me even though I liked the writing, the premise, and the backstory of the characters. You could shuffle the plot points around and nothing would change significantly which makes the horror not have impact.

Felt like a bunch of disconnected short stories. I'd try Luthi again, maybe his short fiction. The premise and setting sounded awesome but the execution didn't keep me engaged unfortunately.

title: Galactic North
author: Alastair Reynolds
review: Glad I read this but the variability on the enjoyment of the stories was a bit high, overall liked more than the Diamond Dogs/Turquoise Days novellas, think the eponymous Galactic North story was a bit overhyped from what I had heard online. Overall still a big fan of Reynolds in general but yeah this isn't going to capstone the whole series in a way that it's a must read.

title: Of War and Ruin
author: Ryan Cahill
review:
A little mixed on this even though overall I really liked it. Felt a bit uneven for me especially depending on the POV and what they're doing at the moment. The highs are high and the lows are low, the boring parts are a bit of a slog as well and a bit bloated, could have used some trimming down. Don't think this book needed to be 1500 pages for any reason. One of the storylines should have been completely cut as should the repeated training sections and there's a lot of repeated phrases sprinkled throughout the book.

That being said and how negative it sounds I did really like a lot of the big epic moments and some of the chapters and POVs were quite good and exciting. Overall this series is entertaining, I don't think it's that deep but it's a fun time and some of the world building and plot is a little under developed. I am looking forward to book 4, a lot was set up here that has a lot of potential, just wish we got even more here for how much of a squirrel squisher this book is.

title: Flux
author: Stephen Baxter
review:
One of the craziest settings for a book that I've read. Definitely a bit challenging in the beginning trying to figure out what was going on and how the world worked and felt like if I had a firmer grasp on the science would maybe make a bit more sense, however as the book went on things made more sense in context and the story was actually fairly straightforward.

This ended up being a page turner and just when I was worried it would start getting stale something new would pop up and grab my interest. I think I liked this more in the context of the previous novels with the background that I know, in isolation maybe this is my least favorite Xeelee book so far. However, the imagination of this series remains to be pretty incredible and really stretches my brain and I feel engaged with the book and trying to make sense of what's going on, the science behind it, and has some really unique locations and vivid scenes that will stick with me.

Very interested in reading Ring as these 3 books have alluded to the eponymous Ring and I want to see what it has in store for us.

title: The Hellbound Heart
author: Clive Barker
review: Great short read to warm up for spooky season, only took me two hours to read. A well put together horror story with no wasted pages and really enjoyed the writing style. Will definitely check out more Barker soon!

title: The Templars: The Rise and Spectacular Fall of God's Holy Warriors
author: Dan Jones

title: Innocent Omnibus Volume 1
author: Shin'ichi Sakamoto
review: Great art, mixed on everything else. The ending was quite strong though and sort of makes me want to try the next one, but we'll see. The way the story is presented also is a bit confusing and it is a bit hard to differentiate some of the characters as a lot are drawn in similar styles

title: Parable of the Sower
author: Octavia E. Butler
review:
Loved this overall. Dystopian book that takes place in 2024-2027 so it was kind of cool to read it in the year it takes place and it's eerily prescient. Butler has an amazing authorial voice that is somehow simultaneously bleak, heavy, angry, but has glimmers of hope. I got Walking Dead and The Stand vibes from this.

The world building details kind of don't make 100% sense but they're not really the focus and it was easy for me to suspend my disbelief a bit but yeah, not completely bought into how the world ended up in this state of disrepair and didn't totally collapse, but that's mainly a background to a more zoomed in and personal narrative.

title: Service Model
author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
review: This was entertaining but it was a bit aimless and overlong. Wish this was trimmed down a bit and had more of a thematic drive to it or went even more in the slapstick crazy direction, it sort of stayed in a middle ground here that didn't satisfy me completely in either direction. I liked this more than Murderbot though. Audiobook narration was good and Tchaikovsky overall is still one of my favorite authors.

title: Return of the Crimson Guard
author: Ian C. Esslemont
review:
This book is a hot mess but I had fun with it for the most part. Showcases a lot of the best and worst of Malazan, definitely confusing as hell and way too many story lines with fast POV changes and too many hidden identities and written in a way where it actively hides information from you. This book is like drinking from a fire hose and can be a bit much at times.

However there's a lot of cool stuff in it and it being complementary to the main series was really nice, it fleshes out some world building only touched on in the main series and continues some plot points with much needed resolutions.

title: Batman: The Killing Joke
author: Alan Moore
review: Very good but a little too short imo. Wish it built up a bit more but what we got was great

title: Neuromancer
author: William Gibson
review: 2.75/5 The atmosphere was good and I liked some parts but everything else was sort of poorly told and unclear in a way that hampered my enjoyment. Sort of felt similar to Phillip K Dick in some ways but I felt like the reveals were not that clear and it got very mixed up in what was happening in the real world or the matrix and what was happening in a dream so I wasn't that invested in the outcome.

title: Vacuum Diagrams
author: Stephen Baxter
review:
Really good capstone to the end of the series, don't listen to reddit and read this first, I don't think this would make much sense without the context of the previous books. I think at a minimum Timelike Infinity and Ring are required reading in the series with the other books are somewhat optional but add additional info and flesh out the timeline more.

The ideas are consistently interesting but can be challenging to figure out what exactly is going on, definitely varied a bit how some of the stories landed and how important they are to the main timeline.

title: Pluto: Urasawa x Tezuka, Vol. 1
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: This was great, bought the whole series and I will be reading it all.

title: Grave Empire
author: Richard Swan
review:
4.5/5 Thank you to Netgalley and Orbit books for an advanced copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

I've read Empire of the Wolf last year and really enjoyed it beginning to end, so I was excited to see what Swan had in store for this world 200 years after the ending of the previous series. Swan met and in a lot of ways exceeded the previous series here, and if book 2 was out I'd pick it up immediately.

He did a great job switching from first person in the EOTW to third person with multiple POVs here and thought the story and pacing benefited from it massively, I was always engaged in what was going on and he was able to tease these big moments and revelations that kept me turning the pages wanting to know what would happen next. This book has a lot of surprising moments and goes in directions I didn't expect but also makes sense given what we know about the world from previous books. Also there's one character here who is such a scumbag and I loved it, easily one of my favorite characters of the year. I thought all of the POV perspectives were interesting and showed the depth and complexity of the world building as well as just having a lot of cool moments that have big implications for the rest of the series.

The horror elements are awesome, probably one of my favorite parts of the book, some truly horrific things happen and I was all for it, really separates this book from other fantasy series and he's really amplified this part from EOTW which I really enjoyed in that series as well.

Swan is one of my favorite new authors in the fantasy genre and he consistently releases books every year, so I'm expecting to continue to get new entries in this series at a regular pace and looking forward to read them (hopefully early!). This is definitely a book 1 in a series but we do have a good stopping point with some but not all the answers and there's plenty to explore as the series continues.

title: Circe
author: Madeline Miller
review: Really good. Kind of yass queen witch power vibes but not overly so and good tying in of existing mythology. Lots of stuff happens but doesn't really build to a crescendo but was engaged by the plot. Also some of the writing is quite good and the audiobook performance is fantastic.

title: The Eye of the World
author: Robert Jordan
review:
Surprised at just how much I enjoyed this. I actually read this book about 20 years ago after finishing what was published of A Song of Ice and Fire at the time and for some reason didn't continue. I didn't remember much about it and sort of ruled out this series as something I wouldn't like but I'm glad I gave it another shot as this is awesome classic fantasy with some really cool world building, high magic, and some epic moments.

Wheel of Time is sort of my last remaining "massive, hugely popular" fantasy series that I haven't read. Definitely will be continuing and excited to read book 2 soon!

title: Leviathan
author: Robert McCammon
review: Have some nitpicks with this entry but overall really enjoyed it, the series definitely fluctuates between intricate mysteries and adventure stories where I personally enjoy the mysteries more. The writing quality is pretty immaculate the whole way through the series and creates a high bar for McCammon to measure up to himself. Highly recommend the series overall and it also has great audiobooks.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review:
Masterpiece, amazing book. So much depth and weight to think about in such a short novel.

I definitely have issues with people who describe this book as "nothing happens". It goes over Mr Stevens' whole life and questions what it means to have dignity and what is important in life. Also it looks at what happens when you feel like you may have took the wrong turns and worry about a life wasted.

The unraveling of the story was brilliant and how it chooses to reveal information to you as it progresses. There were many moments where I was questioning the life philosophy of the characters and the effects it has had on the lives they have chosen to live. The climax I was emotionally engaged, on edge, and heartbroken.

Ishiguro is a master in subtext here and there's a huge amount of the book that rewards a close read between the relationships between the characters but it also felt very accessible and realistic to me and I could vividly imagine the scenes and it's easier to see the shortcomings of these human relationships with the benefit of an outside perspective and Stevens looking back at events in hindsight.

Amazing nuance in the personalities of the characters, how they have changed throughout their lives, and their relationships between one another and how social decorum can often get in the way. Also shows the challenges of capturing those moments to break through the social rituals and really connect with other human beings, especially in the context of pre World War 2 Britain but there's takeaways from this to apply to any situation.

Will definitely be reading more Ishiguro very soon.

title: A Pale View of Hills
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review: This was alright, it was building up and I felt unsatisfied with the ending, there's not any clear answers to some of the mysteries. The Remains of the Day had a lot better payoff where this one felt more unfocused and the themes were a bit muddled to me. Could have used a bit more focus, but I was engaged with the first half of the book quite a bit, it just didn't follow through with something satisfying in the end.

title: The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch
author: Philip K. Dick
review: The most approachable PKD I've read yet, but still has a really cool premise and execution. Will be thinking about this one for quite some time, highly recommend. Very mind melty.

title: Pluto: Urasawa x Tezuka, Vol. 8
author: Naoki Urasawa
review: Series review: Great sci-fi manga that packs a lot into it's succinct package. Don't be deceived by the covers and premise but there's a lot of deep sci-fi themes being explored as well as a lot of emotional and dark moments. Very cool exploration on what it means to be human and memory to name a few. It takes Astroboy and makes it a serious adult story. Urasawa is one of the best at this medium, great stuff.

title: Blood Work
author: Michael Connelly
review: Really good hook and writing. Mechanically very strong police procedural and really dives deep into the evidence in a compelling manner. Have enjoyed every Connelly book I've read so far and wanting to continue Bosch this year. Mccaleb does feel a bit similar to Bosch at times but his motivation for being on this case is very good, his backstory and personal life isn't quite as good as Bosch though. Glad I read this because it is referenced in some of the Bosch books and he's featured in the next one next to Bosch so I wanted context on his book before I read that.

title: The Great Hunt
author: Robert Jordan
review: Seriously impressive. Handles the fallout of the first book and bridges the series to something unique and special. So many great moments and plenty of surprises. Excited to continue. The Wheel weaves as the Wheel wills.

title: Stonewielder
author: Ian C. Esslemont
review: 2.5/5 man this dragged a lot. The set-up was interesting but the middle felt like a slog.
